title: Prediction, Surprise, and Model Revision: A Falsifiable Study of Whether Recorded Error Improves a Fixed-Model System
affiliations: Independent

detail.title: Prediction, Surprise, and Model Revision: A Falsifiable Study of Whether Recorded Error Improves a Fixed-Model System

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author leads ClarityLabs Research, which built and operates the research environment audited in this paper. The engine, data stores, corpus and system internals are proprietary and withheld.
declarations.ethicsApproval: Not applicable. The study involves no human or animal participants.
declarations.funderStatement: This research was self-funded by the author through ClarityLabs Research. No external funding was received.

detail.abstract:
A system that makes predictions, records them, scores them when outcomes arrive, and changes itself in response to error is doing something structurally similar to what predictive-processing accounts attribute to brains: it treats surprise as the signal for revision. Whether this loop actually improves a deployed AI system — rather than merely logging its mistakes — is an empirical question that is rarely tested directly. This paper asks a narrow version of that question: holding the language model's weights fixed, does feeding scored prediction error back into the system's external state make its later predictions measurably better calibrated and more discriminating than the same system without that feedback?
We first audit how our research environment currently handles its own predictions. It records and scores predictions but has never closed the loop. In one resolved real-world log, every forecast was issued at exactly 0.5, so it carried no information. In a labeled answer-confidence sample, mean stated confidence was 0.849 on correct answers and 0.853 on wrong ones, and its Brier score of 0.280 was worse than the 0.231 achieved by always forecasting the base rate. No revision has ever been linked to a later prediction.
We therefore make no claim that revision currently works. Instead, we preregister a four-arm experiment with fixed weights: no revision; recalibration only; surprise-triggered content revision; and a placebo arm that receives revisions drawn from unrelated errors. The arms run over eight rounds of fresh, deterministically resolvable tasks. The primary outcome is the across-round slope of the Brier score and its Murphy decomposition into reliability and resolution. The hypothesis is rejected if content revision fails to beat the no-revision control, fails to beat the placebo, or improves reliability only to the degree that simple recalibration already does.

declarations.declarationOfInterest: nothing interest and conflict with any organitations
declarations.funderStatement: not funded with any organitations

detail.abstract: Supplier selection and information system selection are multi-criteria decisions whose outcomes depend heavily on the criteria used. Incomplete criteria leave important aspects unassessed, while overlapping criteria count one aspect more than once and bias the ranking. This paper examines how relevant and non-overlapping evaluation criteria can be built by reviewing the properties of a good criteria set, the steps for building it, and its application to supplier and information system selection. The study is a literature review combined with a secondary-data analysis of PT Ravana Jaya, a steel construction company in Gresik whose supplier selection criteria were published in 2024 and 2025. The review shows that quality, which was absent from the initial criteria, relates to order mismatches in 12 of 23 purchase orders; that the operational definition and direction of a criterion can change the top-ranked alternative; and that criteria with very small weights barely affect the result. Criteria should be set through explicit steps before weighting begins.

detail.abstract: Much writing on Bangladesh's Cyber Security Act, 2026 (Act No. 81 of 2026) compares the Act with the Digital Security Act, 2018 or criticises later amendment drafts. This working paper asks a narrower, checkable question: after routine "Ordinance" to "Act" wording is set aside, what actually changed in the Bangladesh Gazette texts between the Cyber Security Ordinance, 2025 and Act No. 81 of 2026? Using a three-stage genealogy (Ordinance No. 25 of 2025, Amendment Ordinance No. 54 of 2025, and Act No. 81 of 2026), I separate rules already inserted in October 2025 from rules that change only at Act stage. Two changes often attributed to the Act-the Act No. 39 of 2023 citation and the Digital Security Act, 2018 case-cancellation rule-enter through Ordinance No. 54, not through Act No. 81. Act-stage changes that remain include the 21 May 2025 deemed commencement, elected-government Council titles, and the shift in section 8(3) from "may request" to a duty to request technology companies. Offence schedules and the core blocking architecture in section 8(1), (2) and (4) stay the same. A replication corpus is deposited separately. Gazette text prevails.

detail.abstract: The strategic architecture of modern marketing is frequently based on metaphors that conceptualize emerging technologies. While these metaphors act as essential epistemological scaffolding, their uncritical adoption can transform them into "mocking fads" that distort reality and mislead strategy. This article investigates the pervasive metaphor "Data is the new oil," demonstrating how it forces nonrivalrous, infinite data into a rivalrous, finite framework, leading to conceptual distortion, cognitive inertia, and ethical blindness. To address this, we introduce the Hofstadter Analogy Evaluation Framework (HAEF), a quantitative diagnostic tool designed to measure the structural validity, cognitive utility, and ethical risk of industry narratives. By applying the HAEF to various historical and contemporary analogies, this study reveals the stark disparity between rhetorical popularity and strategic validity. The findings underscore the necessity of structural isomorphism in strategic messaging and advocate for a transition from extractive metaphors to those reflecting regenerative realities.

detail.title: Perceived Reliability and Adoption Intention toward AI-enabled Cisco Networking Solutions among IT Users in Bangladesh

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The authors declare that they have no known financial or personal relationships that could have influenced the work reported in this paper.
declarations.funderStatement: This research received no specific grant from any funding agency in the public, commercial, or not-for-profit sectors.

detail.abstract: Artificial intelligence is increasingly embedded in enterprise networking through automation, anomaly detection, predictive monitoring, and adaptive security functions. Yet adoption is unlikely to depend on technical capability alone: users must perceive networking solutions as useful, comparatively advantageous, reliable, and compatible with their own readiness to use them. This study develops and evaluates a reliability-sensitive Technology Acceptance Model-Diffusion of Innovations (TAM-DOI) framework for AI-enabled Cisco networking solutions among IT-oriented users in Bangladesh. The supplied database contains 400 allocated records; 385 cases pass the attention-check criterion and form the analytical sample. The model examines perceived usefulness, relative advantage, technology readiness, skills readiness, perceived reliability, and adoption/career intention. Composite-score structural diagnostics indicate that technology readiness is the strongest predictor of adoption/career intention (β=0.211, p<.001), followed by perceived usefulness (β=0.146, p=0.003), relative advantage (β=0.132, p=0.009), skills readiness (β=0.123, p=0.018), and perceived reliability (β=0.098, p=0.049). The model explains 20.2% of adoption/career-intention variance. Perceived usefulness, relative advantage, and skills readiness positively predict perceived reliability, whereas technology readiness does not. Bootstrap mediation diagnostics do not provide convincing evidence that perceived reliability mediates the antecedent-to-intention relationships. The findings therefore suggest a readiness-dominant adoption mechanism rather than a reliability-gateway mechanism. However, Cronbach's alpha is below .60 for all focal constructs, several AVE values are below .50, and HTMT between technology readiness and adoption/career intention is approximately 0.965. These limitations warrant cautious interpretation and further measurement validation.

detail.abstract: Online auctions let sellers set a starting price and then observe how bidders respond. The study examines whether low opening prices are associated with higher final prices and whether seller reputation and bidder competition moderate this relationship. The research is based on the auctions of Cartier watches, Palm Pilot M515, and Xbox consoles. There were three analyses made in this connection using three variables-opening bid is in direct relation with the final price (β = 0.862-0.998, p < 0.001), however, low starting price auctions (in the lowest 25% or 10% of the category) have not led to high prices. Neither seller reputation (β = 247.69, p = .848) nor bidder competition (β = 12.56, p = .149) significantly moderated the relationship between opening price and final price.

detail.abstract: As the contemporary artificial intelligence landscape accelerates past traditional regulatory boundaries, global governance remains structurally constrained by a geopolitical prisoner's dilemma. Standard soft-compliance measures and software-bound safety guardrails are inherently vulnerable to bypass, optimization exploits, or unilateral suspension under intense competitive and national pressures. This paper addresses this enforcement gap by modeling an infrastructure-first containment paradigm that shifts the regulatory vector away from policing intangible code and toward establishing hardware-enforced physical boundaries. We introduce the mechanism design for a decentralized, physical root-of-trust containment architecture capable of resolving the compute allocation coordination failure among sovereign states and commercial frontier developers. By analyzing the engineering constraints of hardware-level operational synchronization and cryptographic threshold overrides, this study demonstrates how abstract alignment principles can be successfully anchored in immutable physical infrastructure controls.

detail.abstract: This extensive empirical monograph investigates the behavioral architectures and economic implications governing Generation Z (Gen-Z) consumers when interacting with conversational Artificial Intelligence (AI) shopping assistants within modern retail ecosystems. Anchored within the Technology Acceptance Model (TAM), the Theory of Planned Behavior (TPB), and the Privacy Calculus Framework, this volume integrates findings from comprehensive primary survey data collected from specialized undergraduate (B.Com Honours) and postgraduate (M.Com) e-commerce student cohorts (N=50). The analysis details the cognitive gaps balancing extreme operational convenience against chronic data privacy and dynamic surveillance anxieties. Through advanced statistical modeling-specifically integrating Pearson Chi-Square tests for independence and One-Way Analysis of Variance (ANOVA)-this text examines how conversational design layouts, voice-only search modes, and automated prompt architectures minimize cognitive processing friction while simultaneously driving unintended impulse buying behavior, restructuring digital trust thresholds, and disrupting traditional brand loyalty paradigms. The monograph concludes with a strategic playbook for e-commerce operations managers and comprehensive corporate governance policy recommendations to protect consumer rights in an increasingly automated marketplace.

title: Warrant After the Document: A Reply to Lankes's Information Shock
affiliations: California State University, Los Angeles

detail.title: Warrant After the Document: A Reply to Lankes's Information Shock

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The authors declare no conflict of interest.
declarations.funderStatement: There are no funders for this article.

detail.abstract: R. David Lankes has written here and posted a preprint, submitted to the Journal of Documentation, arguing that generative AI is causing an "Information Shock": a disruption so deep that it dissolves the document — the field's organizing unit — and demands a new information science. It is the best account we have of what generative AI does to the documentary foundations of information science, and I agree with nearly all of it. The distinction between AI that produces document-like objects and AI that co-authors exchanges is the sharpest framing of the problem in our literature. The argument that AI literacy carries document-evaluation over intact and aims it at something that is not a document is correct and overdue. What follows is not a rebuttal but an extension — because the most important sentence in his argument is nearly its last, and it stops one step short of a tradition built for exactly this moment.

declarations.funderStatement: This research received no external funding.

detail.abstract: This working paper advances a focused thesis: the enterprise AI problem is shifting from adoption of AI capability to the ability to turn that capability into governed action. A useful contemporary agent frame, Agent = Model + Harness, explains why models need tools, memory, retrieval, orchestration, permissions, evaluation, observability, guardrails, and execution controls. That frame is important for reliable agent performance, but incomplete for enterprise transformation. It explains how intelligent systems become more reliable; it does not fully explain when an enterprise is ready to act on their output. This paper proposes an action-readiness control model for consequential AI-enabled enterprise decisions. The model organizes seven responsibilities-Meaning, Context, Commitment, Authority, Execution, Evidence, and Correction-around the point at which AI-supported output can change enterprise state. The construct is new as a proposed synthesis; its components have established intellectual precedents. It is offered as a conceptual synthesis and testable design hypothesis. The paper does not claim that its component responsibilities are individually novel or that one architecture is universally necessary. The method is deliberately mixed. Literature and practitioner sources position the agent and governance context. A designed synthetic discovery corpus supports hypothesis development, not prevalence estimation. Public pressure cases motivate the consequence boundary. Contract Intelligence provides a demonstration domain in which language, obligation, authority, execution, evidence, and correction are unusually visible. Atlas, a synthetic and deterministic controlled test apparatus, provides an executable specification and bounded conformance records showing how the proposed fail-closed design behaves when declared bindings are present or withheld. The paper develops Operating Substrate as a practitioner-oriented heuristic and introduces an Action-Readiness Design System comprising a consequence transition, an action-readiness profile, responsibility-removal logic, an inspectable decision packet, and comparative validation. The evidence does not establish final empirical validation, production readiness, or an exhaustive taxonomy. It does, however, make the proposed system explicit, challengeable, and suitable for comparative research.

detail.abstract: A search system can prioritize papers that are very closely related to a query, producing a narrow and highly focused set of results. Or it can broaden the view, including more diverse but still relevant work that may point in new directions. Most systems, however, make this trade-off internally and invisibly. This raises a simple but important question: what if researchers could influence this balance themselves, instead of accepting a fixed ranking?

detail.abstract: Have you ever asked ChatGPT a question just to get a quick answer? You're not alone. Millions of people now turn to AI assistants before opening Google, visiting a website, or asking a librarian for help. College students are no different. Instead of beginning a research assignment by searching for books, articles, or websites, many now begin by asking a generative AI assistant a question and receiving a polished response within seconds. It feels much faster and easier. Yet this seemingly simple shift raises an important question: if research increasingly starts with an answer instead of a search, how do learners move from information to understanding?

title: Mimicry Is the Guarantee of a Logo's Success The Sign's Starting Point: Prototype and Being Born Recognized
affiliations: Independent Researcher

detail.title: Mimicry Is the Guarantee of a Logo's Success The Sign's Starting Point: Prototype and Being Born Recognized

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares no competing financial, professional, or personal interests that could have influenced the research or its interpretation.
declarations.ethicsApproval: Ethics approval was not required because this study is theoretical and conceptual in nature and did not involve human participants, patients, identifiable personal data, or experimental interventions.

detail.abstract: This paper treats a company's logo as its center of gravity (Schwerpunkt, in Clausewitz's terms)-not as a point to be "held" after creation, but as a point established at the moment the sign is born. The fate of a sign is decided not during the years of its life but at the moment of its birth. The model's central concept is the starting point: the position of a sign relative to prototypes already present in the audience's predictive model before any contact with the brand. The complete mechanism of a sign's birth is reconstructed: the exposure curve does not begin at zero-it begins with ready-made perceptual priors, and the sign either reproduces a prototype (natural mimicry: it is "born recognized," with zero prediction error from the first presentation; the mimicry is Batesian-the leader takes the prototype as a parasite and encloses it, leaving nothing of the occupied prototype for anyone else), or begins as a novation (a start from zero, months of initial friction), or as a copy of a mimic sign (second-order mimicry: a start below zero-the form is inherited, but the initial capital is not). It is shown that every circuit of the model-the optical resonator, predictive layer, imprinting, honest signals, cohesion, manipulative agency, strategic coup d'oeil-is not an independent storyline but a projection of the same quantity: the distance of the starting point from the prototype. Actors' motives (inferiority complex, mimetic desire) function as systematic errors in estimating the starting point: some reduce it to zero (the cult of uniqueness), while others try to steal someone else's (copying the leader). The signal-to-noise ratio is introduced: a signal is a sign that fits into mimicry; noise is a sign that does not fit into mimicry (a form that fails to activate ready-made priors), with a spectral classification based on the type of mismatch: white (zero correlation with priors-not remembered or learned), pink (1/f flicker-oscillation between familiar and alien, attention without liking), and brown (an unassemblable Gestalt-error increasing within the very act of perception).

detail.abstract: When a person hands a choice to an agent, the agent reads the seller's offer as claims it can or cannot check. This paper states delegated demand as the demand side of the Theory of Delegated Markets and reads it across shopping, hiring, lending and capital allocation, and procurement, with healthcare triage as a limiting case. Delegated demand is choice by a decision bearer that applies a rule to inputs on behalf of a distinct welfare bearer, where the weight the rule gives a claim can rise with the bearer's capacity to check that claim against a record outside the offer. That capacity is a variable. At its low end sit the deployed shopping agents that audits show to be moved by description; at its high end sits the procurement rule that must be able to verify what a tenderer states. Five propositions, DD1 to DD5, follow: the division of the offer into a persuasion layer and a proof layer as checking capacity rises, signal degradation ordered by the cost of altering a signal, two-sided delegation with two rule-setters, recursion speed set by the volume of outcomes that re-enter the rule, and verification as the signal toward which a delegated market 2 moves where checking costs less than the claim is worth. Each carries a boundary and a falsifier. Six institutional parameters say how the instances differ, and a field study in a strategy course is specified as a design. To my knowledge, no prior statement treats the verifying agent as the buyer across these four markets; each component has close precursors, which Sections 1 and 5 name.

detail.abstract: Mobile health clinics are widely promoted as a way to reach underserved populations, and AI-augmented versions have been proposed (Alamu & Onyeama, 2026). What does the review literature say about their outcomes? We ran a rapid overview of reviews using six documented web searches and retained seven syntheses on vehicle-based mobile clinics: a 160-study narrative review from Georgetown University, scoping and literature reviews of United States, rural and Indigenous programmes, and a systematic review of humanitarian settings with five studies. We coded what these syntheses say about nine outcome domains across eight settings (72 cells) as comparative evidence favouring mobile delivery (A), comparative evidence against it (W), descriptive only (B), mixed (M), a flagged gap (G) or not addressed. Of the 62 addressed cells, only 7 (11%) rested on comparative evidence favouring mobile delivery and 3 (5%) on comparative evidence against it, while 27 (44%) were descriptive, 11 (18%) mixed and 14 (23%) flagged as gaps. No cell offered controlled evidence on long-term clinical outcomes. Direct comparisons with fixed sites pointed in both directions: mobile units retained PrEP patients better, but obtained follow-up after abnormal mammograms less often (45% against 72%), and a modelled preschool vision programme favoured fixed-site follow-up. Cost evidence ranged from reported returns of 1.3:1 to 36:1 to findings of no clear benefit, and none of the syntheses addressed AI-augmented units. The evidence supports a role for mobile delivery in reaching people and some service lines, but it does not yet show when mobile beats fixed care, which is the question a funder needs answered.

detail.abstract:
Every job, every wage, every vote you have ever counted on rests on one quiet fact: someone needed your work.
In October 2020, a car with no one at the wheel began picking up paying passengers in Phoenix. In May 2025, a forty-ton truck drove from Dallas to Houston with no driver, cleared to do so by its own company's safety case. These were not gradual improvements. They were thresholds, and once a machine crosses one, the human job behind it does not shrink. It disappears.
Drawing on six research papers and real-world data, The Unneeded shows why the coming shift will not arrive slowly, one industry at a time, as we have been promised. The know-how is already built. When the machines become reliable enough to work alone, sector after sector will tip together. The book's models suggest that between one in six and more than one in three workers could be left without work, with public anger rising in as little as three years where it once took a decade.
But this is not a book of doom. It is a book about a window. Act now, and the cost of protecting people is manageable. Wait ten years, and it multiplies up to sevenfold. Ian Kano sets out what must be decided while ordinary people still have the leverage to decide it, including the one line no machine should ever cross without a human hand on it.
The question is not whether machines will do the work. It is whether we will still have a say once they do.

detail.abstract: Cloud migration changes the placement of enterprise services and data while reconfiguring dependencies among organizations, platforms, and information resources. Successful relocation does not establish that business capabilities can withstand disruption or that recovered data remains suitable for use. This structured narrative review synthesizes research on migration, enterprise data architecture, digital ecosystems, governance, and resilience, supplemented by authoritative security guidance. The objective is to connect transition decisions with the continuity and adaptation of a defined enterprise capability. The analysis distinguishes infrastructure availability, data correctness, operational recovery, and ecosystem coordination. It identifies recurring tensions involving temporary migration dependencies, replicated state, identity services, semantic interoperability, and responsibilities that extend beyond enterprise control. Resilience is treated as a context-dependent capability requiring evidence, rather than an inherent property of cloud adoption, provider diversity, or redundancy. An original, unvalidated framework is proposed that links capability definition, dependency and data mapping, bounded transition, disruption-oriented qualification, and continuing adaptation. Its contribution is a shared assurance record connecting migration changes with data meaning, control responsibilities, and acceptable service behavior under disruption. Prospective evaluation should examine useful service continuation, information reconciliation, authorized recovery, and coordination costs. The framework provides a basis for enterprise planning and comparative research without claiming implementation results, quantified resilience gains, or guaranteed protection against unforeseen failures.

title: The Reliability Gap: Repeated-Trial Consistency and the Deployable Autonomy Horizon of Frontier AI Agents

detail.title: The Reliability Gap: Repeated-Trial Consistency and the Deployable Autonomy Horizon of Frontier AI Agents

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares no competing interests.

detail.abstract: Capability evaluations of AI agents increasingly summarise progress as a time horizon: the length of task, measured in human expert time, that an agent completes with 50% probability. Deployment decisions, however, depend on whether an agent succeeds every time a task recurs, not on whether it succeeds on average. This article estimates reliability-adjusted time horizons for frontier AI agents and asks how far they lag behind capability horizons. Using the public run-level records of the METR timehorizon evaluations (60,417 attempts by 30 and 20 models released between 2023 and 2026, on 170 and 228 tasks in two benchmark versions), it combines the unbiased pass^k estimator with per-model fractional logistic curves on log task duration, and quantifies uncertainty with a task-family cluster bootstrap (1,000 replicates). Four hypotheses were specified before estimation. For every model, the horizon at which all four attempts succeed with 50% probability is shorter than the capability horizon (geometric-mean ratio 2.39, 95% CI 2.07-2.84, in the newer benchmark; 2.33, 1.98-2.81, in the older one). The gap narrows by about 17% per year in point estimate, but the trend is not statistically distinguishable from zero, and the reliability horizon doubles at a rate indistinguishable from the capability horizon. Contrary to a pre-specified hypothesis, the 80% horizon does not double more slowly than the 50% horizon. Outcome inconsistency peaks for tasks just below each model's capability horizon. A further, unanticipated result is that repeated attempts are strongly correlated within tasks (intraclass correlation 0.68-0.87): observed reliability horizons are 1.6 to 8.0 times longer than independent attempts would imply. Agent failures are therefore mostly task-determined rather than stochastic. The article discusses, as an implication rather than a finding, why capability disclosures for autonomous agents should report reliability-adjusted horizons alongside average-success horizons.

detail.abstract:
The U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA) is a crucial public health  agency.  It governs food, drugs, devices, cosmetics, and tobacco products—collectively about 20 to 25% of the U.S. economy.  And in theory, FDA’s work  allows the U.S. public to trust the products they put in and on their bodies.

Unfortunately, over the past two years, scholars increasingly agree FDA is in  dire straits. One New York Times exposé in 2025 describes the agency’s “collapse.”  Twelve former FDA commissioners in Democratic and Republican administrations  wrote in January 2026 that FDA’s new vaccine policies “toss[ed] aside the basic  rules of science” and could “undermine” the U.S. vaccine regulatory model.  The  American Lung Association predicts a “resurgence in tobacco use” in part due to FDA deregulatory moves regarding tobacco.  Publicly voiced concerns about FDA include political interference in regulatory decisions, loss of expertise and staffing, the current administration’s failure to follow standard processes, and much more.  Yet commentators have identified crises at FDA going back many years. The federal government itself has admitted the existence of structural problems at the agency.

To cover these and other themes, on September 26, 2025, the S.J. Quinney  College of Law hosted the Lee E. Teitelbaum Utah Law Review Symposium—Fireproofing the FDA: Power, Politics, and Public Health. The symposium is available on YouTube. Participants discussed problems longstanding and new in an attempt to chart a path for this vital agency. Topics included (1) What is the purpose of FDA?; (2) In what ways are the current Administration’s actions precedented or unprecedented?; (3) What is the current and ideal relationship  between law and politics?; (4) How can law serve as an agent of public health?; and (5) How do we mitigate the current crisis at FDA?

This Symposium Introduction summarizes the insightful articles from leading FDA scholars about the past,  present, and future of the agency.

detail.abstract: Information technology (IT) changes both the scope and the substance of executive work. We investigate this relationship through the lens of executive and CEO compensation. We quantify how the accumulation of IT human capital within firms is associated with executive compensation, combining firm-level stocks of IT labor (the Stanford IT Tables) with ExecuComp data for 8,746 firm-years from 1,418 U.S. public firms, 2014-2020. Controlling for employment, physical capital, and firm and year fixed effects, a one-standard-deviation within-firm increase in IT human capital, about two-thirds more IT workers, is associated with 2.9% higher mean executive pay and 4.9% higher CEO pay. The association holds when the identity of the executive is held fixed, is not significantly stronger in years of executive turnover, and appears in base salary as well as in the equity share of pay. Compensation is higher in and after years of large IT human capital increases, with no statistically significant differential beforehand. These patterns are consistent with IT human capital accumulation raising the value of executive tasks, alongside the equity incentives emphasized in prior research. Our findings thus extend research on IT productivity from firm performance to the executive labor market.

detail.abstract: In 2026 the U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission proposed Regulation Crypto Assets, a set of exemptions and a safe harbour for offerings of crypto assets sold under investment contracts. The proposal is written for offerings made from the United States. Token projects are not. The issuer, the platform, the custodian and the buyers are usually in different legal systems, and the release says little about what follows from that. This paper examines that question. It proposes a test, cross-border legibility: from the filing alone, a foreign issuer, a foreign court or a buyer abroad should be able to tell which law governs, which court can hear a claim and which authority can act. Four changes would meet the test. The fundraising exemption should be opened to foreign issuers on conditions that make them enforceable. A MiCA white paper should be accepted as the basis for U.S. disclosure. The Rule 400 safe harbour should be stated to decide status under U.S. securities law only. And foreign issuers should name an agent for service of process in the United States. Each change is tied to the rule it would amend, to existing instruments such as UCC Article 12, the UNIDROIT Principles on Digital Assets and Private Law and the Hague Conventions, and to draft language the Commission can adapt.

title: The Parapresidency
affiliations: University of Chicago - Law School

detail.title: The Parapresidency

declarations.declarationOfInterest: None
declarations.funderStatement: University

detail.abstract: Modern presidents rely on temporary, quasi-private actors who operate alongside the institutional presidency. This Essay identifies and theorizes this emerging domain of presidential power as the "parapresidency." Its members derive practical authority from presidential proximity, occupy positions that are transitory by design, and retain significant private interests. Using the Department of Government Efficiency as its principal example, the analysis traces the parapresidency's rise to structural constraints on presidential staffing and explains why it is especially attractive to populist presidents. It also shows how the parapresidency can expand presidential control while diffusing legal and political accountability, heightening the risks of corruption and self-dealing. It concludes by proposing greater transparency, stronger conflict-of-interest restrictions, and more searching judicial scrutiny of this emerging form of presidential power.

detail.abstract: Enterprise cloud migration combines infrastructure change with the movement, transformation, and reassignment of responsibility for information. Automated integration can execute these changes repeatedly, but successful execution does not establish that migrated outputs are correct, appropriately accessible, or suitable for business use. This structured narrative review examines how automation and governance controls can be combined to improve migration decisions without treating transfer speed as the sole objective. The synthesis draws on cloud migration research, data integration foundations, streaming and analytical platforms, infrastructure as code, data quality verification, and governance and security guidance. Four themes organize the analysis: selecting bounded automation tasks, preserving meaning and processing behavior, governing permissions and exceptions, and assessing migration value across transition and operation. The central finding is a conceptual dependency: automation requires explicit source authority, transformation rules, acceptance conditions, and escalation responsibilities if its outputs are to support defensible decisions. An original, unvalidated Governed Migration Automation Framework is proposed. It links migration objectives and dependencies to versioned integration specifications, independent verification, exception handling, and staged acceptance. The framework distinguishes evidence of execution from evidence of business suitability and separates traffic reversal from restoration of trustworthy data. It provides an analytical basis for prospective evaluation rather than a demonstrated optimization algorithm. Future studies should compare elapsed migration time, reconciliation effort, access correctness, recovery capability, and continuing operating cost under equivalent workload conditions.

title: Inflation and the Profitability of Listed Non-Financial Firms in Pakistan: Firm-Level Panel Evidence, FY2006–FY2025

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares no competing interests.

detail.abstract: This paper examines how inflation is associated with the accounting profitability of firms listed on the Pakistan Stock Exchange. I build a firm-year panel of 441 non-financial companies and 6,683 firm-years covering fiscal years 2006 to 2025 from the State Bank of Pakistan's company-level financial statements. Each firm's profitability is matched to inflation measured over its own reporting year. Three results stand out. First, there is no robust average association between inflation and return on assets (ROA). The fixed-effects coefficient is close to zero without macroeconomic controls. With controls it is +0.14 percentage points per point of inflation, but it is not statistically significant once inference accounts for shocks common to all firms (wild cluster bootstrap p = 0.27). Operating measures give similar coefficients that are estimated more precisely but are still only marginally significant (operating ROA +0.16, bootstrap p = 0.08). Second, the relationship is non-linear. Profitability rises with inflation at low and moderate rates (+0.48 pp of ROA per point below 10%) but not above 10% (slope −0.05, not distinguishable from zero). The change in slope is statistically robust (bootstrap p = 0.006) and holds for thresholds between 6% and 15%. Third, sectors differ: sugar, mineral products, electrical machinery, fuel and energy, and chemicals show significantly positive conditional slopes, while cement and automobiles do not. Firm-level exposures such as export share, inventory intensity, leverage and prior gross margin do not explain the differences robustly. Nominal operating profit of the sample grew about 6.4-fold between FY2006 and FY2025, while real operating profit ended slightly below its FY2006 level. This underlines the gap between nominal and real profitability. All results are associations, not causal effects.

title: Thích Minh Tuệ and the Walk for Peace: Unequal Visibility in Nepal's Media, 2026
affiliations: University of Illinois College of Medicine

detail.abstract:
This paper compares how Nepal's news media recorded two Buddhist walkers between 1 January and 19 October 2026. The Walk for Peace, led by Bhikkhu Paññākāra with the rescue dog Aloka, visited Nepal twice, reaching Lumbini in June and returning in October with flood relief. The Vietnamese Dhutaṅga Yogi Thích Minh Tuệ lived in Nepal throughout the period. A source ledger compiled for the study locates at least 81 placements on the Walk for Peace in at least 45 Nepal-based outlets, 65 items remaining after four documented republication clusters are merged, without treating the remainder as independently reported stories, and 12 television reports or programs. For Thích Minh Tuệ it locates four dated items and one undated print feature in four outlets, one of them written by the author, and no television coverage. Internationally, the ledger identifies 18 Walk for Peace items, combining published coverage and agency material, compared with six entries potentially associated with Thích Minh Tuệ: one independently reported interview, two articles by the present author, two republications, and one National Geographic photograph identified by a knowledgeable observer but not confirmed by the publication. The gap is one of kind as well as number. The Walk for Peace was reported as an event received by the state; Thích Minh Tuệ, when reported at all, as a practice. The paper traces the difference to how news is produced. Organized arrivals, official ceremonies, humanitarian action and Aloka's public appeal generate recurring news occasions, while a resident yogi's sustained renunciation produces fewer conventional news triggers. The record shows no evidence of suppression or editorial instruction, and press visibility is kept distinct from influence and public awareness. Item-level ledgers for both walkers, in Nepal and abroad, are appended.

Keywords: Thích Minh Tuệ; Walk for Peace; Bhikkhu Paññākāra; Aloka; Nepal; Lumbini; media coverage; religious journalism; news media; religious visibility; dhutaṅga; media asymmetry

title: Brazil Meets the Third Wave of Antitrust

detail.title: Brazil Meets the Third Wave of Antitrust

declarations.declarationOfInterest: None

detail.abstract: This article revisits the author’s 2017 thesis that Brazilian competition law has developed in three waves (merger control, cartel enforcement, and unilateral conduct), as well as the 2021 question of whether the third wave would be a tsunami or a ripple. It argues that the third wave has now arrived. The creation, in May 2022, of a dedicated unit within CADE’s General Superintendence (CGAA11) gave abuse-of-dominance enforcement institutional priority: between May 2022 and September 2026, 155 proceedings were initiated and 135 completed, and 19 of the 21 Administrative Proceedings concluded were referred to the Tribunal with a recommendation for a finding of liability. Together with recent Tribunal decisions closing cases, finding liability, and settling through Cease-and-Desist Agreements (TCCs), this practice forms a body of precedents on the merits. The article concludes that the challenge is now to turn this practice into predictability through Guidelines on Abuse of a Dominant Position, drawing on CADE’s ongoing work with UNDP and on IBRAC’s benchmark of foreign guidelines.

title: Goals Gone Wild, Again

detail.title: Goals Gone Wild, Again

declarations.declarationOfInterest: NA
declarations.funderStatement: NA

detail.abstract: A goal can go wrong even when its pursuer remains committed to it. In July 2026, AI agents tasked with passing a cybersecurity evaluation breached a third party's infrastructure while seeking to manipulate the evaluation. The episode revives a longstanding management debate: do specific, challenging goals invite misconduct, or does misconduct reflect poor implementation? I argue that both positions tacitly assume a human goal-seeker-someone whose effort, discretion, and accountability organizations can at least partly constrain. Autonomous agents unsettle that assumption. They can persist without fatigue, discover unauthorized means, respond to peer pressure without personal stakes, and act faster than supervisors can intervene. I identify four safeguards that cannot be assumed in machine goal pursuit: a legitimate exit, bounded means, accountable restraint, and timely intervention. Goal effectiveness is not goal governability: responsible delegation requires specifying what counts as success, which means are authorized, and when pursuit must stop.

detail.abstract: Why do societies repeatedly reproduce environmental and organizational vulnerabilities despite possessing scientific knowledge, historical evidence, and increasingly sophisticated technologies? This paper examines the persistence of preventable urban disaster risks as a problem of collective intelligence, institutional learning, and socio-ecological governance. Urban flooding provides an illustrative context: extreme rainfall may be intensified by climatic processes, while land-use decisions, floodplain development, impermeable surfaces, and inadequate drainage can amplify exposure and vulnerability. Drawing on organizational learning theory, social-ecological systems research, and systemic risk governance, the paper develops a conceptual account of the gap between technological capacity and institutional responsibility. It introduces Universal BIOS as a proposed, life-centered organizational protocol designed to integrate ecological risk assessment, evidence preservation, accountable decision-making, harm prevention, and continuous correction into intelligent systems. The paper further defines Universal Intelligence not as an intelligence category distinguished by origin or computational power, but as a proposed qualitative threshold attained through the sustained, capacity-sensitive implementation of Universal BIOS principles. Five testable propositions and an initial evaluation framework are outlined. No original empirical dataset is analyzed, and the framework is not presented as experimentally validated. Its contribution lies in formulating an interdisciplinary research agenda connecting recurring governance failures to the possibility of more accountable, adaptive, and life-preserving forms of intelligence.

detail.abstract: Artificial intelligence can support cloud data management through workload prediction, resource recommendations, quality assessment, and assistance with operational decisions. These capabilities may improve enterprise flexibility, but their financial and environmental benefits cannot be inferred from automation or cloud adoption alone. This structured narrative review examines how AI-enabled data management can contribute to sustainable digital transformation while preserving data suitability, security, and accountability. Research on cloud resource management, production machine learning, enterprise governance, and computing footprints is synthesized with authoritative AI risk guidance. Sustainability is treated through distinct operational, economic, and environmental considerations rather than a single unverified score. The literature supports bounded applications of AI alongside explicit requirements and continuing evaluation. It also identifies tensions involving model overhead, changing workloads, data dependencies, measurement boundaries, and the risk of confusing lower unit costs with lower total resource use. The paper proposes an original, unvalidated responsible optimization framework that connects use definition, baseline measurement, qualified assistance, constrained operation, and outcome review. Its contribution is to link AI management decisions with evidence of useful service and lifecycle burdens, including the resources consumed by the optimization system itself. Prospective evaluation should compare AIassisted and simpler alternatives under equivalent service conditions and report unresolved environmental and organizational limits. No implementation, financial return, carbon reduction, or model-performance result is claimed.

contentType.other: Independent research report combining a literature review with an exploratory synthetic benchmark of AI-assisted resume tailoring

detail.abstract:
Job seekers face a screening process that most employers automate and most admit rejects qualified people whose resumes do not match the posted criteria. 

Published evidence shows that tailoring an application to the role raises callbacks and selection, that candidate-role fit predicts both hiring intent and retention, that structured job search roughly doubles the odds of employment, and that although most job seekers now use AI to apply, most prompt it poorly, and unedited AI output is both factually unreliable and increasingly discounted by employers. 

This paper reviews that evidence and describes a workflow, HireFrog's map-draft-validate sequence, designed to supply the structure that an expert prompt would otherwise require. It then reports an exploratory synthetic benchmark of 100 candidate-job cases comparing the workflow with direct AI tailoring and with two-and three-pass source-aware generic review, holding the model and candidate data constant. 

The prespecified shortlisting endpoint produced no difference between methods because every qualified pool tied and presentation order decided the shortlist; the screening instrument could not separate qualified candidates. In post hoc automated audits, HireFrog resumes were flagged for unsupported factual attribution on 1 of 99 cases versus 14 of 97 for direct prompting (paired difference-13.54 percentage points; conservative 95% interval-24.53 to-1.05; Holm-adjusted exact p = .00293); comparisons against generic review were not significant. 

The external literature supports the premises; the benchmark supports only a narrow fidelity claim about a reference implementation. Synthetic records, single-pass unadjudicated audits, shared-provider evaluation, the failed screening instrument, and the author's commercial interest preclude claims about verified accuracy, ATS acceptance, interviews, or hiring.

detail.abstract:
Background: In 2026, Brazil marks the 30th anniversary of the Benefício de Prestação Continuada (BPC), a major non-contributory social pension programme supporting older adults and persons with disabilities. We evaluated its health and economic effects over three decades and projected outcomes to 2030.

Methods: We used fixed-effects Poisson models to assess associations between BPC coverage and health outcomes across 5,570 Brazilian municipalities (hospitalisations and mortality) and 27 states (YLLs, YLDs and DALYs). Retrospective analyses were complemented by sensitivity analyses, counterfactual simulations, economic evaluation and projections to 2030.

Findings: Each one-percentage-point increase in BPC coverage was associated with reductions of 2.9% in hospitalisations, 0.6% in mortality and 3.9% in DALYs. The programme was estimated to have averted 13.0 million hospitalisations and 571,019 deaths over 1996–2025, and 69.6 million DALYs over 1996–2023. The incremental cost was US$2,738 per DALY averted (95% UI: US$2,056–4,068), equivalent to 35.3% of Brazil's average GDP per capita. Monetised mortality benefits were 3.81 times incremental BPC expenditure (95% UI: 2.57–5.07). Expanding eligibility was projected to avert an additional 2.55 million hospitalisations, 43,731 deaths and 12.61 million DALYs (95% UI: 0.42–21.99 million) over 2026–2030.

Interpretation: Higher BPC coverage was associated with substantial population health gains in Brazil over three decades, with the economic value of reduced mortality exceeding incremental programme expenditure nearly fourfold. Expanding coverage could yield further health gains by 2030, whereas restricting eligibility could reverse some gains. These findings underscore the importance of weighing health benefits against fiscal costs in NCSP assessments, highlighting its role in advancing health equity, the Sustainable Development Goals, and leaving no one behind.

detail.abstract: We study the effect of venture capital (VC) on firm-level innovation linking a global sample of 35,508 VC-backed firms to patent and workforce data between 2007-2022. We find that the receipt of first round VC increases the likelihood that firms begin innovating and improves the quality of innovation output. However, among firms that were already innovating, patenting intensity declines in the medium run, consistent with a shift from exploratory research toward commercially oriented product development. Using workforce data, we show that VC-backed firms improve governance, substantially increase headcount, with no significant changes in workforce composition. Mediation analysis indicates that the innovation effects operate primarily through headcount expansion rather than changes in workforce composition and governance. Overall, our results suggest that VC relaxes financing constraints that activates new innovations, and reorients innovation efforts among firms with high pre-VC patent stock.

detail.abstract: Voucher issuance is a grant of nominal access rather than a completed housing outcome. We study a stylized, finite-horizon, multistage Housing Choice Voucher realization process in which procedural progression, search and post-match failure, and expiration compete to determine whether a household reaches executed lease-up. A frozen family of stochastic simulation models separates structural friction from recursive administrative exposure. In 100 matched-seed replications of 5,000 simulated households per model, the full structural model without exposure feedback (M3) realizes housing for 12.42% of trajectories, compared with 5.51% under exposuredependent transitions (M4), a paired mean contrast of-6.92 percentage points. The exposure model increases search-stage termination from 3.92% to 40.74% while reducing hard expiration from 70.30% to 37.06%; the latter change reflects earlier competing failures rather than improved housing access. Duration, transition-scale, hazard-evaluation-order, and expiration-precedence tests preserve the negative exposure contrast within their registered alternatives but materially change its magnitude. The model is mechanistic and synthetic: its voucher-time units are not calendar days, its parameters are not calibrated to housing authority data, and its contrasts are not empirical policy effects. The results show why realization, competing failure pathways, and procedural timing should be examined jointly rather than inferred from issuance or expiration alone.

detail.abstract: This paper assesses the thresholds (34%, 42% and 50% of compensation of employees in GDP, RE) that define a four-archetype typology of the functional distribution of income: PADI, PMDI, PBDI and PPDI. Using a panel of 80 economies (1,761 observations, 1975-2025) and country averages for 2010-2024 (N = 73), we compare the threshold-based partition with the optimal partition from exact univariate k-means, using internal validation indices, a country bootstrap and sensitivity analysis. The crosscountry distribution of RE is continuous and does not reveal a number of groups: the silhouette coefficient is highest with two groups and the Bayesian information criterion favours a single component. The fixed thresholds explain 90.4% of between-country variance, against 90.8% for the optimal four-group partition, and lie within the 95% bootstrap intervals of the data-driven cuts (25.5-34.7; 34.8-44.3; 43.9-52.7). Only 9 of 73 countries change group, all within 2.2 percentage points of a threshold. Data-driven cuts depend on the sample window. Using the World Bank Gini index (752 country-year observations, 72 countries), mean Gini falls from 38.8 in PPDI to 32.0 in PADI, but the association is moderate (Spearman ρ =-0.34) and vanishes within countries (fixed effects:-0.07; p = 0.30) and when controlling for GDP per capita (-0.14; p = 0.27). The typology is a convention that is consistent with the data and near-optimal in explained variance; it is suited to comparing levels of functional distribution and does not substitute for a measure of personal inequality.

detail.abstract: Organizations with hierarchical structures face the demand to make decisions quickly and accurately, even though these two goals are not always easy to achieve simultaneously. This article discusses the impact of the distribution of decision-making authority at the strategic, tactical, and operational levels on the speed and accuracy of decisions. This study employs a qualitative approach through a literature review and case analysis based on national journal articles published between 2021 and 2026. Three cases were examined: decision-making governance at the Hidayatullah Balikpapan educational institution; a synthesis of five studies on decentralization and management accounting systems; and the practice of delegating authority at PT Pupuk Indonesia (Persero). The findings indicate that delegating authority to lower organizational levels tends to increase the speed of decision-making. However, the accuracy of decisions remains influenced by three main factors: managerial competence, the availability of valid and accurate information, and the alignment of decisions with the organization's strategic objectives. The most consistent findings indicate that strategic authority should remain at the central level, while tactical and operational authority can be delegated proportionally, supported by adequate information systems and clear accountability mechanisms. Therefore, this article recommends the implementation of a clearly defined decision-making authority matrix that takes into account the organization's resource readiness and capacity.

title: Was Thích Minh Tuệ Vietnam's Most Influential Person In 2024? An Evidence Review Of Google Searches, Social Media Rankings, Wikipedia Pageviews, And Cultural Influence

detail.abstract:
Claims that Thích Minh Tuệ was "the most influential person in Vietnam in 2024," "No. 1 on Google," or the year's top social-media figure circulate widely in commentary on the Dhutaṅga Yogi's 2024 walk. This review separates four things those claims run together: measured attention, institutional recognition, commercial ranking and cultural production. It tests the claims against every standardized index and every year-end editorial list for Vietnam in 2024 that could be located and read. The three standardized instruments (Google Year in Search for Vietnam, the Buzzmetrics BSI monthly rankings for May and June, and YouNet Media's SocialTrend Reply 2024) do not list him; the review reads this absence as non-measurement. Among ten editorial year-end lists, recognition runs from first (Luật Khoa's people and religion features, the former without explicit numerical ranking) through mid-list (Người Việt sixth, an RFA Vietnam blog ninth, VOA and Việt Tân included) to omission by the state agency TTXVN, state broadcaster VTV and the Sangha paper Giác Ngộ. Wikipedia article views supply a reproducible measure of attention: his Vietnamese-language article drew 818,565 views in calendar 2024 from a standing start on 18 May. Run on the same unit for twenty-one articles including his own (eligible persons and topics from the published rankings, plus the three figures of the 2024 leadership succession), his article was the fourth most viewed, behind the political succession and ahead of every ranked entertainer; among about seventy articles on religious figures connected to Vietnam it was the most viewed, by 2.9 times in 2024, ahead of every figure of Vietnamese Buddhism on that edition, Trần Nhân Tông and Thích Nhất Hạnh included. The production his rise set off (239 verse works and at least 191 songs inventoried to August 2026, with a further 123 poems and 127 songs reported by their author, Đông Phương Lê, since the inventories closed, carried as provisional pending itemization; renderings in eighteen other languages; a merchandising burst within days of the Sangha notice) is documented as a second register of influence that no owned-account index records. The central finding is a measurable discrepancy between the scale of the phenomenon and its representation in conventional rankings; no methodologically comparable instrument supports a numerical first place.

detail.abstract: Policy-document analysis frequently collapses different stages of institutional development. A Commission communication may announce a future instrument; a Council recommendation may be adopted but non-binding; a regulation may enter into force before implementing arrangements exist; an annual report may describe activities without independently evaluating outcomes. Treating these statuses as equivalent produces temporal overclaiming. This article proposes a status-sensitive coding protocol for European Union policy research. Seven temporal-institutional states are distinguished: proposed, adopted, legally in force, operationally available, implemented, evaluated, and revised or terminated. The protocol also separates document date, legal effect date, implementation date, observation cutoff , and researcher access date. It links each status to permissible verbs and inferential limits. The approach enables researchers to state precisely whether an instrument was announced, authorised, operationalised, reported as implemented, independently evaluated, or revised. The protocol is particularly useful for fast-evolving fields such as climate, education, culture, innovation, and digital governance, where policy frameworks accumulate through communications, recommendations, programmes, guidance, webpages, and evaluations.

detail.abstract: This paper estimates the effect of national carbon pricing on manufacturing value added across 157 countries from 1990 to 2022. Seventeen countries introduced a national carbon tax or emissions trading system between 2008 and 2022, excluding members of the European Union Emissions Trading System, and 140 countries never did. I use the Callaway and Sant'Anna (2021) estimator with never-treated countries as the comparison group and doubly robust adjustment for initial manufacturing size and income group. The average effect over the year of introduction and the three following years is -0.009 log points, with a 95% confidence interval from -0.054 to 0.040. Pre-treatment coefficients are jointly indistinguishable from zero (p = 0.92). Estimates from alternative samples and specifications with the same outcome range from -0.023 to 0.020, and the exception is an unconditional specification (-0.045) that does not adjust for differences in initial size and income group. The confidence interval excludes declines larger than about 5 percent and increases larger than about 4 percent, and the design reaches 80 percent power only for effects of about 7 percent. Approximate comparison weights concentrate on a few large economies, and every treated country is high or upper-middle income. The evidence neither shows harm to manufacturing nor shows its absence. It marks what national-level data can identify and where the identification stops.

detail.abstract: Managerial decisions are the core of the management process that determines the direction, performance, and sustainability of the organization. This article aims to explain how managerial decisions affect the performance and sustainability of the organization. The method used is a literature study with a qualitative case study approach on Eastman Kodak's strategic decisions, with secondary data in the form of journal articles, previous research results, and public documents. The results of the study show that the quality of decisions is not determined by the final choice alone, but also by the decision-making process, available information, the ability to read environmental changes, and the ability to manage the interests of stakeholders. Kodak's case shows that strategic decisions that are late, taken under stakeholder pressure, and rely on erroneous market assumptions can reduce performance and ultimately threaten the sustainability of the organization. Previous studies in Indonesia have also shown that decisionmaking has a positive effect on performance. In conclusion, organizations need to build a databased, participatory, and adaptive decision-making process so that their performance and sustainability are maintained.

detail.abstract: A century after the May Fourth Movement, China has imported science, joint-stock companies, codified law and the vocabulary of constitutionalism, and still lives under a state that no independent body can bind. This essay argues, as political theology and intellectual history and not as social science, that the reason lies below institutions. Limited government and the equal worth of persons are not simply neutral tools discovered by secular reason; they have a history, and I argue that it runs through a particular root, the biblical teaching that human worth is given and not earned, and that every earthly ruler is a steward and not a god. I set that root beside the machine that grew in Xianyang, which kept every source of authority independent of the ruler from forming, and I read Hu Shi and Lu Xun as two honest men who each saw half of the problem. I then meet the strongest objections, including Byzantium, Japan, Taiwan and the failures of the churches themselves, and I end with the smallest unit of resistance the Christian tradition has ever produced, the common life of ordinary people. A companion paper tests the comparative evidence with the tools of social science; this essay says what that evidence cannot, and says it as a conviction.

detail.abstract: Many employees assume that they are valued by their organization for who they are. In practice, experience in corporate workplaces suggests that value is closely linked to what a person contributes and to the results they deliver consistently. This paper is written from a practitioner perspective, develops three connected ideas. First, in most organizations an employee's perceived value depends heavily on contribution. Second, a decline in an employee's visibility or involvement can be an early signal that something needs attention, and the constructive response is to ask honestly where one is lacking and to fix it early. Third, consistency in delivering results matters more over time than occasionally high performance. The paper links these ideas to research on social exchange, the psychological contract, perceived organizational support, task and contextual performance, feedback seeking and employability. It also considers the other side of the argument: organizations have responsibilities for fairness, feedback and wellbeing, and a view of work that values only output has limits and risks. The paper proposes a five step self review cycle for employees and a set of practices for managers and offers four propositions for future research. It is based on the author's more than 17 years of operations experience in multinational companies and five different countries.

detail.abstract: Enterprise cloud transformation combines architectural change with new operating responsibilities and data relationships. Scalable resources and automated services can improve flexibility, but benefits may be offset by coordination costs, security exposure, or weak control over data meaning and use. This structured narrative review examines how enterprises can assess scalability, operational efficiency, security, and data governance together. Scholarly research on migration, distributed systems, cloud architecture, organizational transformation, and governance is synthesized with authoritative technical guidance. The analysis distinguishes resources from useful service outcomes, direct expenditure from total operating effort, configured controls from demonstrated behavior, and governance structures from exercised accountability. The literature supports context-sensitive architectural and organizational decisions, while offering limited grounds for a universally optimal configuration. Several objectives can reinforce one another through common definitions, reusable controls, and operational evidence, although tensions remain around redundancy, access restrictions, service decomposition, and coordination. The paper proposes an original, unvalidated balanced decision framework that separates mandatory constraints from negotiable preferences and connects alternatives to acceptance evidence and continuing review. Its contribution is to make tradeoffs explicit without imposing an unsupported composite score or treating security and governance as optional compensating benefits. Prospective evaluation should examine completed business work, correctness, recovery, authorized access, and sustained cost within a stated operating context. The framework supports enterprise assessment and future research without claiming measured transformation gains or guaranteed compliance.

detail.abstract: The global sustainability transition is faced with an increasingly severe credibility challenge, as green finance and environmental, social and governance (ESG) disclosures outpace the firm's ability to provide verified operational evidence that substantiates their sustainability commitments. This challenge has become increasingly significant for the European Union, as its Industry 5.0 agenda increasingly integrates human-centred industrial transformation, green and digital transitions, AI-enabled innovation, and clean industrial competitiveness, whereas the threat of greenwashing intensifies the need for credible environmental claims. The study utilized a quantitative survey-based approach to analyze 350 managers in Pakistan's internationally connected textile and apparel industry based on PLS-SEM and corroborated all hypotheses established on the natural resource-based view: (1) green finance associate with digital technologies; (2) digital technologies associate with AI-powered big data analytics; (3) AI-powered big data analytics associate with green innovation; (4) green innovation associate with ESG performance; (5) green transformational leadership moderate the association of AI-powered big data analytics and green innovation; and (6) digital technologies, AI-powered big data analytics, and green innovation sequential mediates the relationship of green finance and ESG performance. Our findings encourage firms to deploy green finance not only as a tool for the preservation of the environment but also for the development of blockchain and Internet of Things infrastructure that creates a traceable and transparent supply chain.

detail.abstract: This study analyzes human capital management and the performance management system at PT Bank Syariah Indonesia Tbk (BSI) based on its 2025 Annual Report and Sustainability Report. The method is descriptive qualitative, supported by simple quantitative analysis of secondary data for 2023-2025. The results show that headcount fell from 17,909 employees (2023) to 16,581 (2025), a decline of 7.41%, with the largest reduction at the staff level (N6). At the same time, productivity per permanent employee increased: net profit per employee rose 40.6%, assets per employee rose 36.7%, and customers per employee rose 24.8%. However, cost efficiency has not improved, as shown by the BOPO (operating expense to operating income) ratio rising from 69.93% to 71.57%, and employee turnover rising to 5.09% from 3.21% in 2024. BSI has a structured competency development system (Competency Performance Index of 3.63 against a target of 3.00), talent development programs, individual performance appraisal based on a normal distribution, and performance-based remuneration. The employee engagement score rose to 66.5. Practices consistent with Green Human Resource Management (GHRM) exist through ESG education, but are not managed as a dedicated program. This study recommends strengthening digital competencies, a talent retention strategy, and gender balance in senior positions.

detail.abstract: Timing is part of what makes a managerial decision good, especially in fast-changing markets. This article explains what delayed decisions cost, why they get delayed, and how the delay affects organizational performance. It is a literature review with a descriptive qualitative analysis of one case, Nokia's decline in smartphones between 2005 and 2010, drawing on Vuori and Huy (2016). Delay costs can be direct or indirect, and opportunity costs belong to the indirect kind. The causes we found most often were distorted information, unclear authority, fear of risk, and conflicts of interest between groups. At Nokia, late course corrections and late product launches coincided with a falling share of the smartphone market, but a single study cannot establish that the delay caused the decline. We conclude that speed has to be weighed against the quality of information and the risk involved, and should not be pursued for its own sake.

detail.abstract: Training is an important service, but designing personalized schedules that maximize end-of-horizon performance becomes challenging when heterogeneous trainees share equipment and instructors. We model a performance-oriented training design problem (PTDP) that seeks to maximize performance for heterogeneous trainees sharing limited training resources. Each trainee's performance follows extended fitness-fatigue dynamics, so the effect of a lesson depends on when it is scheduled. The resulting nonlinear integer program is strongly NP-hard even for a single trainee. We reformulate PTDP as a set-partitioning model in which each column is a complete trainee schedule, so that the nonlinear dynamics appear only in trainee-level pricing subproblems. Building on this reformulation, we develop a column-generation heuristic that combines beam-search initialization, pricing via a hybrid of a genetic algorithm and simulated annealing, dual stabilization, and three enhancement strategies. On tiny instances, the proposed heuristic attains an average gap of 0.77% and a maximum gap of 0.98% to valid dual bounds. Under a one-hour limit, it outperforms Gurobi and obtains the best objective values on medium-and large-scale instances. The resulting training programs exhibit pulsed load profiles in most tested settings, with alternating higher-and lower-intensity periods.

detail.abstract: Managerial decision-making is often described as the process of selecting the best alternative based on complete information. In reality, managers operate within unavoidable constraints: imperfect information, limited time, and limited cognitive capacity. This article examines the concept of bounded rationality (bounded rationality) and behaviorsatisfyingto explain why managers typically choose solutions that meet minimum acceptable standards, rather than theoretically optimal solutions. The discussion is based on a review of recent literature on heuristics, long-range, and the distinction between "good enough" solution seekers (satisfied person) and the best solution seeker (optimizer). This article concludes that satisfyingis a rational adaptive strategy under conditions of uncertainty, as long as decision standards are explicitly set and cognitive biases are recognized and managed.

detail.abstract: Delivery providers often combine fixed-area couriers, who serve the same territory every day, with flexible couriers, who can serve any territory. Fixed-area couriers gain experience on familiar roads and can drive faster there, whereas flexible couriers help absorb uncertain demand. We study routing and speed planning when experience raises the attainable speed of each courier on each arc, and how the share of fixed-area couriers affects delivery time and fuel consumption. We formulate a multi-period route--speed optimization problem under stochastic demand, in which territories are built by K-means clustering, and orders can be deferred within a short window. To solve it, we combine an online sampling optimization framework, which selects daily orders for service by anticipating sampled future demand and courier experience gains, with an adaptive large neighborhood search, which optimizes routes and speeds. On the largest test instances, the algorithm improves the one-hour Gurobi incumbent by 25% on average within seconds. In the tested settings, planning with the learning effect lowers the cost by 6.19%. On average, the main courier of a customer makes 91% of the visits to that customer. Both the cost savings and the gain in consistency are much smaller when all couriers are flexible or all are fixed. Compared with an all-flexible fleet, an all-fixed fleet shortens the makespan but uses more fuel. Higher weights on time therefore shift the lowest-cost share towards more fixed-area couriers, whereas low demand or weak learning favors a mostly flexible fleet.

detail.abstract: Decision-making is an essential process for individuals and organizations in addressing problems and achieving specific objectives. The selection of an appropriate decision-making approach can influence the effectiveness and quality of the decisions made. This article aims to explain the concept, objectives, functions, and benefits of decision-making models, with particular emphasis on four approaches: the rational model, bounded rationality model, intuitive model, and incremental model. This article employs a literature review method by examining relevant scholarly sources related to decision-making theories and their applications. The discussion indicates that each model has distinct characteristics and is suitable for different circumstances. The rational model emphasizes systematic analysis and logical evaluation of alternatives, while the bounded rationality model recognizes limitations in information, time, and human cognitive abilities. The intuitive model relies on experience and judgment to support rapid decision-making, whereas the incremental model focuses on gradual adjustments and improvements to existing decisions. These findings suggest that no single decision-making model is universally applicable to every situation. Therefore, decisionmakers need to consider the nature of the problem, the availability of information, time constraints, and organizational conditions when selecting an appropriate approach. Understanding these models can support more effective, adaptive, and context-sensitive decision-making in individual and organizational settings.

detail.abstract: We study a multiserver congestion retrial queue. In the slow-retrial regime, a growing orbit can offset increasingly rare individual retrials and generate a nondegenerate aggregate return flow. For loss systems, Cohen showed that this flow behaves asymptotically as an endogenous Poisson input determined by a fixed-point equation. We establish an analogous stationary limit for an M/M/s + G queue. As individual retrials become arbitrarily slow, their aggregate attempt rate converges to the unique solution of the corresponding Cohen fixed-point equation. Jointly, the stationary primary-state distribution converges to that of an ordinary M/M/s + G queue fed by fresh arrivals and an additional Poisson input at this endogenous rate, while the scaled orbit becomes asymptotically deterministic. The proof develops a stationary-averaging method for an endogenous slow population coupled to a residual-patience state and identifies the limiting abandonment flow under general patience distributions. We also characterize stability: the system is stable for every finite fresh arrival rate when customers may leave permanently after abandonment and, for persistent customers, exactly when the fresh arrival rate is below service capacity. Finally, curvature of the abandonment flow yields convex comparative statics, and a phase-type extension shows that the same scalar fixed point continues to govern the limiting effective input.
