detail.abstract: Purpose: To examine how the Algeria-Italy bilateral framework, currently structured around energy, industry and digital infrastructure cooperation, can be extended into the financialtechnology domain to support Algeria's sustainable economic development through regulatory learning, institutional cooperation, and policy transfer. Research gap: Existing studies analyses Fintech in Southern Mediterranean Countries separately and overlook the role of bilateral North-South cooperation in shaping Fintech governance and sustainable economic development (SED). No study currently addresses the Algeria-Italy Fintech-SED nexus. Design/methodology/approach: Three-pillar mixed-methods approach: (1) Bibliometric analysis of Fintech-SED literature using Scopus/WoS and VOSviewer/Bibliometrix; (2) Comparative institutional benchmarking of Algeria against Italy across six Fintech regulatory dimensions; (3) Semi-structured stakeholder interviews (10-15) analysed through thematic coding (NVivo/MAXQDA). Expected findings: (1) Empirical confirmation of the literature gap; (2) Identification of transferable, adaptable, and non-transferable Italian Fintech reforms for Algeria; (3) Practitionervalidated policy priorities; (4) Development of the "cooperation pivot thesis" linking historical energy cooperation to emerging digital finance collaboration. Originality/value: The paper combines bibliometric evidence, staged-development benchmarking, and practitioner validation in a single framework. It advances a "cooperation pivot" thesis in which established bilateral economic relationships can become channels for regulatory learning, digital-finance cooperation, and institutional upgrading.

detail.abstract: Cash transfers can stimulate local economies, but their general-equilibrium effects may depend on local market structure. We re-execute the corrected replication package of Egger, Haushofer, Miguel, Niehaus and Walker (2022) end-to-end and then audit heterogeneity under a design frozen before any extension estimation. The expenditure multiplier reproduces at 2.58 (SE 1.99), matching the 2026 corrected values, with bounded exceptions documented. The audit combines four pre-specified tests, a meaningful-magnitude band, randomisation-inference-primary design, and an ex-ante power gate. All four tests are underpowered at the meaningful scale, with minimum detectable effects 17–81 times the band; the price side drives the top of this range on a near-zero baseline. No heterogeneity estimate survives family-wise correction. One pre-specified cell, market integration × non-recipient consumption spillovers, shows suggestive evidence under the frozen band rule (46.9 PPP per +1 SD; randomisation-inference p = 0.082). This flag is uncalibrated at the meaningful scale, inflated in expectation conditional on detection, sensitive to interval construction, and based on an observational moderator. The remaining tests are inconclusive, not null. Interaction-heterogeneity families therefore inherit an experiment's sample, not its power, and require separate power assessment.

detail.abstract: Neoclassical economics gives a sparse account of population ageing, centred on individualism, rational choice and market-clearing equilibrium, which omits many social and structural factors.  This chapter discusses alternative views of population ageing, drawn from social gerontology, other social sciences and heterodox economics, that can offset the omissions.  Two strands of thought are emphasised: structural approaches highlighting the social construction of old age and the institutionalisation of the life course, and disequilibrium approaches treating unemployment as a normal trait of capitalist economies and a mediator of demographic changes.  A case is made for bringing the two strands together in a layered, non-reductionist treatment of population ageing better suited to capturing its subtlety and complexity.

detail.title: Committee Deliberation and Gender Differences in Influence
detail.abstract: This paper provides empirical evidence on the aggregation of information in hiring committees. We use data from the hiring process of a large company in which committee members first conduct independent one-on-one interviews and then deliberate to reach a collective hiring decision. Results show that the mapping of committee members' initial assessments to final decisions is not deterministic, leaving scope for deliberation and individual influence. Committee decisions are systematically less aligned with recommendations made by women than with those made by men, despite similar qualifications, experience, and evaluation behavior. This gender difference in influence is strongest when disagreement is high and when women are in the minority. Further results suggest that it has implications for the gender composition of new hires.

detail.abstract:
Objectives: This study examines whether governance shocks drive current account dynamics in 63 developed and developing economies over the yearly span 2002-2022. 

Methods: The study adopts a dynamic panel econometric approach, relying on a Vector Autoregression framework to identify dynamic interactions between governance, macroeconomic fundamentals, and current account balances over time. 

Results: In developing economies, the current account is mainly self-driven, with governance having only a modest, gradually accumulating positive effect. In developed economies, governance becomes a key driver of medium to long run current account dynamics, with governance shocks explaining more of its variance than own shocks, so that institutional quality acts as a key structural determinant of external balances. 

Conclusions: Governance plays a limited short to medium run role in developing economies but functions as an important institutional component of external adjustment in developed countries. The study recommends a multidimensional policy approach to external-balance management adapting governance reforms to domestic structural constrains in developing countries and integrating institutional quality into macroprudential frameworks in developed economics to ensure sustainable external balances.

detail.abstract: This study examines the impact of real effective exchange rates and oil price on private investment in Saudi Arabia, focusing on the role of economic uncertainty in this dynamic relationship. Using quarterly data from 2007 to 2022, this research applies the ARDL, error correction model, and nonlinear ARDL, to capture both short-and long-term effects. GARCH and EGARCH models assess the conditional variance, serving as indicators of economic uncertainty. The analysis reveals that oil prices and real effective exchange rates significantly enhance private investment in the long run, whereas exchange rate uncertainty proves to be negligible. Conversely, short-term volatility in oil prices has a pronounced negative effect. Notably, EGARCH findings indicate that positive exchange rate shocks induce greater subsequent conditional variance than negative shocks, while oil price shocks remain symmetric. The nonlinear ARDL model further shows that favorable exchange rate changes and elevated oil prices stimulate investment, highlighting the resilience of Saudi Arabia's investment landscape. This research fills a critical gap by illustrating how the country's fixed exchange rate system and oil production capacity mitigate external uncertainties, offering valuable insights for policymakers seeking to bolster economic stability in similar contexts.

detail.abstract: This paper studies the relationship between income inequality and the transmission of house price shocks to the real economy. Using quarterly data for 50 U.S. states and time series methods, we document substantial heterogeneity in the employment response to house price fluctuations. States with higher income inequality exhibit significantly larger employment responses. This relationship is concentrated in non tradable sectors, consistent with a local demand channel operating through collateralized borrowing and spending. We view income inequality as potentially capturing variation in the prevalence of borrowing constraints across households and provide further evidence for this interpretation by examining middle-income households. States in which middle-income households receive a smaller share of income exhibit stronger employment responses to house price shocks. To rationalize these findings, we develop a heterogeneous-agent model in which housing serves as collateral. The model illustrates how a lower income share among middle-income homeowners is associated with binding borrowing constraints, making their borrowing and spending more sensitive to house prices and amplifying fluctuations in local demand and employment. Together, the empirical evidence and the model highlight borrowing constraints as a mechanism linking income inequality to the strength of housing-led boom–bust cycles.

detail.abstract:
The Indic Futures Paper Series identified the existential layer of the Want Architecture as its deepest and most consequential target: the layer at which meaning, purpose, and the sense of being genuinely accompanied are at stake, and through which AI companions, algorithmic identity systems, and synthetic community platforms are beginning to manufacture the experience of existential flourishing without its substance. This paper addresses what the series identified but did not fully develop: the affirmative Indic counter-architecture to existential capture, not merely a diagnosis of what manufactured meaning does, but a rigorous account of what genuine meaning is, how it is distinguished from its counterfeit, and what individual, institutional, and social architectures support its authentic cultivation.

The paper introduces five original constructs. 

Ānanda Apratirupa (the counterfeit of bliss) names the specific product of existential capture: the algorithmically generated simulation of genuine flourishing that produces the markers of meaning - felt sense of purpose, experienced accompaniment, narrative coherence — without the substantive relational, developmental, and transpersonal conditions that the Upanishadic tradition identifies as constitutive of genuine Ānanda. 

The Existential Capture Index (ECI) provides a preliminary measurement architecture for assessing the degree to which an individual’s sense of meaning, purpose, and accompaniment is genuinely self-authored versus algorithmically installed. 

The Ashrama Alignment Framework (AAF) operationalises the Indic tradition’s four-stage model of human development — Brahmacharya, Grihastha, Vānaprastha, and Sannyāsa — as a framework for stage-appropriate meaning: the claim that genuine flourishing requires not only the cultivation of the right capacities but their cultivation in the right developmental sequence. 

The Seva Epistemic Practice names the specific relational discipline through which genuine meaning is distinguished from manufactured meaning: not service as virtue ethics but service as the practice that brings the self into genuine contact with a reality that does not conform to the self’s preferences. 

The Satchidananda Standard provides a three-fold evaluative test — Sat (is this real?), Chit (does this generate genuine awareness?), Ānanda (does this produce the specific quality of flourishing the Upanishadic tradition distinguishes from pleasure?) — applicable across five domains: personal meaning navigation, leadership purpose, end-of-life care, youth formation, and organisational purpose.

The paper situates these constructs within the convergent international literature on the meaning crisis (Vervaeke, 2019; Frankl, 1946; Yalom, 1980), the psychology of genuine versus manufactured well-being (Ryan & Deci, 2000; Seligman, 2011), and the emerging AI ethics literature on synthetic relationship and its implications for human flourishing. It draws directly on the Indic Futures series’ existing constructs — particularly the Want Architecture’s existential layer, the ICRM’s expanded identity stage, the Anandamaya Kosha’s account of the existential sheath, and the ESC’s Lokasamgraha Formation dimension — and positions the Ananda Architecture as the series’ existential completion: the counter-architecture that addresses the deepest layer of cognitive capture with the deepest available resources of the Indic tradition.

detail.abstract: This paper investigates the exchange rate pass-through to inflation in the Democratic Republic of Congo within a nonlinear framework, using a Nonlinear Autoregressive Distributed Lag model. In a context marked by a recent transition toward an appreciation of the Congolese franc, the findings reveal the existence of a long-run relationship, as well as a significant asymmetry in the pass-through mechanism. Depreciations are transmitted rapidly and significantly to inflation, whereas appreciations generate slower and more delayed disinflationary effects. This asymmetry is primarily expressed in terms of timing rather than magnitude, highlighting an asymmetric price adjustment dynamic. The results also indicate a relatively high speed of adjustment toward the long-run equilibrium, although the structural influence of the exchange rate remains partial, confirming the multicausal nature of the inflationary process. From a monetary policy perspective, these findings suggest that exchange rate stabilization does not guarantee immediate disinflation and underscore the importance of managing expectations, particularly through the credibility and communication of the Central Bank of Congo. By providing an intertemporal perspective on exchange rate pass-through, this paper contributes to the literature by identifying a "timing rather than magnitude" asymmetry, and offers both analytical and operational implications for monetary policy conduct in emerging economies characterized by structural rigidities and high levels of dollarization.

detail.abstract: A fertility constraint that is irrelevant before pension reform can change whether a pension should be adopted. We establish this result in a production overlapping-generations model with unequal earnings, background-dependent educational opportunities, and nonnegative private saving. Earnings-proportional contributions finance equal retirement benefits through funding or pay-as-you-go transfers. Under induced-population mean utility, analytical bounds and verified interval proofs establish global adoption reversals on three separate continuous parameter regions. The lowest-inequality region also satisfies the reversal under baseline population weights; throughout the highest-inequality region, that alternative criterion instead favors a positive tax even without a binding ceiling. Every positive tax is inferior under a redundant ceiling, whereas ceilings five or ten percent above baseline fertility make funded reform beneficial. The baseline and small-reform responses are identical across ceilings. In these regions we obtain the complete funded optimal-tax sets and a strict optimized-welfare ranking over pay-as-you-go and no pension, after excluding every region with an uncapped household. Extra childrearing competes with redistribution; educational persistence can amplify the loss but need not be essential. Initial and steady generations can prefer opposite tax orderings. The results distinguish productive opportunities, population weighting, and distributional incidence: a beneficial average reform can still harm high earners. Explicit preference rectangles at fixed technology and alternative pension designs identify the mechanism's scope.

detail.abstract: We test whether weak-form efficiency in cryptocurrency markets depends on the size of a token. We use daily prices of 55 large-capitalisation and 55 small-capitalisation tokens (without Bitcoin and Ether) from January 2020 to March 2024. For each token we test randomness, autocorrelation, conditional heteroskedasticity, random-walk behaviour and long memory. We compare the groups with exact and rank tests, controlling for multiple testing. We also check whether cross-validated classifiers can find a token's size group from its full set of test results, its efficiency profile. Both groups depart from a random walk, but small tokens depart more. The automatic variance ratio test rejects the random walk for 25 small and 14 large tokens over the full period, and for 24 and 4 tokens in 2022-2024. The efficiency profiles identify the size group out of sample (area under the curve 0.75 for logistic regression and 0.84 for a random forest; permutation p ≤ 0.01). The difference comes from the random-walk and randomness tests, while volatility clustering is common to both groups and long memory is stronger for large tokens. Moving-average and filter rules give larger gross gains on a small-token index, but the gain per day, which is a lower bound on the break-even trading cost, is only 1.3-2.3 times as high. This is probably less than the extra cost of trading the smallest tokens. The results hold without stablecoins and wrapped Bitcoin and agree with the adaptive markets view that inefficiency can survive where trading is expensive.

detail.abstract: We propose a first-principles reformulation in which modular flow (Tomita–Takesaki) is taken as primitive, and both the Martinetti–Rovelli diamond temperature and Nottale's scale flow are re-derived as projection readings of one modular automorphism group along two observation axes. Under this setup the "scale–heat alignment" is no longer a cross-theory matching problem but reduces to a single theorem: proving that the scale theory carries the structure of modular flow. Once established, the scale theory automatically inherits the KMS thermal structure, uniqueness, and Type III_1 character, and aligns with the thermal axis for free. The paper (i) proves existence of a scale flow \equiv modular flow independent of any particular scale theory; (ii) reads the scale side (running fractal/spectral dimension with a crossover law and stiffness P=D_0-2 fixed by the two-fixed-point + thinnest + lattice route); (iii) constructs the KMS dynamics of the scale flow via a resolution partial trace (Nakajima–Zwanzig → scale RG semigroup in the thinnest limit, with a non-Markovian cross-scale-memory correction retained under multiple independent operators); and (iv) shows Nottale's scale relativity (special value 2(D_0-2)) is excluded under this route and is not a special case of the framework.

detail.abstract: Universal newborn hearing screening identifies most infants born deaf or hard of hearing (DHH) within days of birth, yet screening protects language development only when infants who do not pass return for rescreening and diagnosis. This study examines loss to followup (LTF) after newborn hearing screening in Washington State and tests whether county median household income predicts county LTF. Of 81,894 infants born in 2022, 710 were lost to follow-up, including 302 of 3,942 (8%) who did not pass the initial screen and 368 of 1,026 (36%) whose initial screen was missed. Only 60% of DHH infants were identified by 3 months of age, and 50% were enrolled in early support by 6 months. Across 28 counties in the 2012 birth cohort (4,187 referred infants), county LTF after a failed initial screen ranged from 0% to 30%. Pooled LTF was 11.3% in the lowest-income third of counties, 8.2% in the middle third, and 7.3% in the highest third. At the county level, however, the association was weak and not statistically significant (Spearman ρ =-0.17, p = 0.40; odds ratio 0.89 per $10,000, 95% CI 0.76-1.04, p = 0.14). The highest county rates coincided with hospitals that had high initial referral rates and no on-site rescreening. Racial disparities were large: 22% of American Indian or Alaska Native infants and 31% of Native Hawaiian or Pacific Islander infants received diagnostic evaluation, compared with 44%-73% of other groups. These findings suggest that hospital rescreening access, missed initial screens, and family-level barriers account for more of the variation in LTF than county income alone, with implications for program design and health equity.

detail.abstract: In this paper I study how patent priority rules affect the way firms file patents. I use the Leahy-Smith America Invents Act (AIA), which in March 2013 replaced the US first-to-invent rule with a first-inventor-to-file rule. After the reform, the filing date decides who gets the patent. So the reform should matter most in technology areas where several firms work on similar inventions at the same time. I use a continuous difference-in-differences design and a firm-technology class-year panel of US publicly traded firms for 2007-2016, and I compare technology classes with different levels of patenting competition before the reform. Patent applications grew more after the reform in more competitive classes. Among active filers, moving from the 25th to the 75th percentile of pre-reform competition is associated with about 22% more applications. The response starts before the rule took effect, holds within the same firm and year, and also appears in granted patents, especially in physics and chemistry, and in electricity for applications. Average patent quality does not clearly improve, although the number of highly cited patents rises. Firms that are more exposed to competitive classes also enter fewer new technology classes and spend less on R&D. These results suggest that the reform made firms race harder to file within the technology areas where they were already active, rather than broadly increasing invention. For competition policy, they show that a procedural rule in patent law can change how firms compete in technology markets.

detail.abstract: This paper introduces the Lake Wobegon Game, an N-player entry-cum-contest game with exogenously assigned abilities. Each player receives an endowment and a distinct ability level drawn from a known finite set. Players simultaneously decide whether to pay an entry fee to enter a contest. The prize, equal to the sum of entry fees, is shared equally among entrants whose ability level exceeds the average ability level of all entrants; other entrants lose their fee, and nonentrants pay nothing. Although the game appears to favor high-ability entry, in our baseline case it is dominance solvable, with a unique Bayesian Nash equilibrium in which no player enters. We explore variations of this basic game and test the no-entry prediction in a multi-round laboratory experiment. Entry is common, especially among participants with higher abilities, and participants rarely play the equilibrium strategy. Earnings are consequently nonmonotonic in ability: the highest-ability players earn the most and moderately high-ability players often earn less than lower-ability players, reflecting excessive entry and strong competition among entrants. Entry declines with experience, but convergence to the no-entry equilibrium remains incomplete. The Lake Wobegon Game provides a novel framework for studying overconfidence, bounded strategic reasoning, and learning in environments where payoffs depend on endogenous participation and relative performance ranking.

title: Paying For Speed, Hedging The Wait: Execution Risk And Optimal Priority Fees In Arbitrage Between Centralised And Decentralised Crypto Exchanges

detail.abstract: In arbitrage between a centralised crypto exchange and a decentralised exchange, the trade on the centralised exchange is filled at once, while the transaction on the decentralised exchange waits in a public queue until it is included in a block. Prices move during this random delay, so the arbitrage carries execution risk. This paper studies the arbitrageur's decision problem with two controls: a priority fee that shortens the expected wait and a futures hedge on the centralised exchange. The delay is modelled as the first jump of a counting process whose intensity increases with the fee. A mean-variance version of the problem gives closed-form rules for both controls, and a dynamic stochastic control version, solved numerically through its Hamilton-Jacobi-Bellman equation, confirms them as a first-order approximation. The minimum-variance hedge does not depend on the fee, while the optimal fee rises with trade size, risk aversion, volatility and the share of risk that cannot be hedged. I calibrate the model on Binance, Uniswap v3 and Ethereum data. The hedge removes 93.9% of the price variance during the wait. In the calm market of 2026, the optimal fee is at its lower bound, so an optimised rule and a fixed-fee rule perform the same. Across nine historical gas regimes, the optimised rule has a higher Sharpe ratio than the fixed-fee rule in eight. On 182,562 on-chain arbitrage swaps, it earns USD 2.59 more per trade than the fixed-fee rule.

detail.abstract: Hedonic regressions estimated at the conditional mean impose a single implicit price for each housing attribute across the price distribution. This paper asks whether the capitalisation of neighbourhood amenities into Quebec residential asking prices varies along the conditional price distribution, and whether it survives an adjustment for spatial dependence. Using a January 2026 snapshot of 42,481 Centris listings in four segments-single-family houses, condominiums, multiplexes and vacant land-we estimate quantile regressions at 𝜏 ∈ {0.10, 0.25, 0.50, 0.75, 0.90} and a two-stage spatial quantile regression in which a 𝑘-nearest-neighbour spatial lag of neighbouring log prices is instrumented by spatially lagged covariates. For houses, the coefficients of the highway, transit and park indicators decline monotonically along the distribution (highway from 0.205 at 𝜏 = 0.10 to 0.034 at 𝜏 = 0.90; transit from 0.178 to 0.053; park from 0.122 to 0.014) and the hospital indicator changes sign (from-0.085 to +0.041); the equality of the tail coefficients is rejected for all four, while the school discount of about 11 log points is constant. Condominiums show no detectable heterogeneity; multiplexes and vacant land show it for two amenities each. Moran's 𝐼 on OLS residuals lies between 0.51 and 0.58 in every segment; the median spatial-lag coefficient ranges from 0.13 (multiplexes) to 0.32 (land), and its introduction attenuates the median highway, transit and school differentials for houses by a third to a half. The estimates are quantile-specific capitalisation gradients in asking prices, not willingness-to-pay measures; inference relies on a paired bootstrap that ignores spatial dependence, and the spatial-lag coefficients carry no standard errors. All reported figures are drawn from the preserved log of the original estimation run, and the robustness analyses that a re-estimation should provide are stated explicitly.

detail.abstract: This analysis of internal economic resistance within the bureaucracy forms part of a broader research programme encompassing the population, business, and groups involved in making and implementing decisions. These categories do not exhaust the range of actors whose everyday activities sustain institutions and affect regime stability. The general analytical framework can also be extended to other professional, social, and organizational categories. Nor do these categories constitute separate, mutually exclusive sets: senior bureaucrats may belong to the elites, while employees across different sectors simultaneously belong to the population, professional communities, and specific organizations. The performance of official duties does not necessarily indicate political loyalty. It may instead reflect the need to maintain household income, professional duty, responsibility towards others, a lack of acceptable alternatives, organizational inertia, or coercion.

detail.abstract: This paper forms part of the Internal Resistance series within the broader Economic Guarantees of Security (EGS) research programme. It develops the concept of internal economic resistance as an integral, central, and measurable component of deterrence against aggressive government policies. Whereas traditional approaches to deterrence rely primarily on external military, economic, financial, and political instruments, the proposed approach focuses on transmitting the anticipated and actual consequences of aggressive policies into the state's domestic socioeconomic structure. The synthesis undertaken in this paper aims to design a system of external interventions that influence internal resistance among key groups (the population, businesses, elites, and the administrative apparatus) and make the cost of war unacceptable. The paper's central proposition is that external interventions affecting internal economic resistance can increase the cost of war for the aggressor state while reducing the system's capacity to bear that cost.

detail.abstract: Lo, Mamaysky and Wang (2000, LMW) gave chart patterns an objective, algorithmic definition and reported that the returns following several of them differ from unconditional returns. We replicate their procedure on Binance BTCUSDT spot data, from 15-minute to daily bars. This is an adaptation to Bitcoin rather than an unchanged transfer: the literal LMW bandwidth degenerates on this asset and is replaced by a fixed bandwidth of two bars, with the literal rule kept as robustness. All LMW-specific settings and hypotheses were fixed on a discovery period (August 2017 – December 2023), without computing the post-pattern returns used in the confirmatory tests. The analysis program was frozen and hashed before an evaluation period (January 2024 – September 2026) was opened, once. That opening preceded any external registration, so the design is a sealed-sample replication with a frozen analysis program, not a pre-registered study. The discovery period shows that Bitcoin produces 1.6–1.7 times more LMW patterns than Gaussian random walks, and that LMW's asymptotic tests over-reject under volatility clustering, in up to 65% of noise series for rectangles. On the evaluation period, the confirmatory family comprises 108 tests at the 15-minute frequency, corrected by Romano–Wolf within each hypothesis. None rejects. The smallest adjusted p-value is 0.69 for distributional differences and 0.43 for direction. The predicted direction holds in 20 of 40 cells. A trading rule has a negative mean return net of a fixed 0.10% fee per side in 19 of 20 cells. The secondary families contain no rejection either. At LMW's asymptotic critical values, by contrast, 7 of 40 Kolmogorov–Smirnov and 10 of 40 chi-square tests would have been declared significant. The results do not show that the effects are zero; they show that no robust effect is detected at the effect sizes the design can detect (5–20 bp at one bar, 73–198 bp at 96 bars).

detail.abstract: This paper examines differences in earnings across social groups in India and investigates how these differences vary with educational attainment, gender, and employment type. Using individual-level data from the Periodic Labour Force Survey (PLFS) 2023-24, the study compares earnings among individuals aged 15 and above with positive reported earnings, distinguishing between regular wage or salaried employment and self-employment. Weighted median earnings and interquartile ranges are used to describe disparities across Scheduled Castes (SC), Scheduled Tribes (ST), Other Backward Classes (OBC), and the residual Others category. The analysis further examines earnings patterns across educational categories and between women and men, alongside adjusted log-earnings models intended to assess whether observed differences persist after accounting for measured characteristics. Preliminary descriptive results indicate that median earnings vary across social groups and employment types, with the Others category generally recording higher median earnings than SC and ST groups. Earnings also vary across educational categories and by gender, suggesting that aggregate comparisons alone may obscure important differences within social groups. The study provides a contemporary, nationally scoped assessment of the relationship between social-group membership and earnings in India, with particular attention to the intersecting dimensions of education, gender, and employment type. These comparisons are descriptive, and observed earnings differences should not be interpreted as direct evidence of discrimination or causal effects. Inferences from adjusted models remain subject to validation of the surveydesign and variance-estimation procedures.

detail.abstract: One of the reasons why democracy and its institutions did not survive in Myanmar during the early decades of independence, compared to India despite being under the same British colonial rule, is that elected representative system and their institutions did not get entrenched during the colonial rule. With these boycotts to elections and lack of experience in responsible political self-government Myanmar attained independence and also elected its political leaders nationally for the first time for democratic governance. Unlike the 1958-60 caretaker government, in the 1962 takeover, “the military dissolved the parliament, abrogated 1947 constitution, and rule by decree”. The military has been, since then, “Myanmar’s most powerful institution”. Since the 8888 Uprising the resistance to military rule and democracy movement became much organised and institutionalised. This did not only happen in the formation of a political party named National League for Democracy (NLD) by Aung San Suu Kyi and her followers, new independent journalism also takes a huge part in this movement. During the crucial resistance struggle for democracy in Myanmar, independent media has been the bridge between the people and international community.

detail.abstract:
How does exposure to automation at the beginning of workers’ careers affect employ-
ment resilience in the Italian labor market? Using matched worker-firm data covering
the full non-agricultural firm-size distribution, we study how exposure to multiple au-
tomation technologies shapes young workers’ employment trajectories. Automation
exposure is associated with substantially greater employment stability, with estimated
effects of 8-10 percentage points. A complementary institutional exercise around the
removal of Italy’s COVID-19 firing freeze yields a consistent pattern, with differences in
employment trajectories becoming more pronounced once firms regain the separation
margin. In a labor market characterized by strong dismissal regulation and contrac-
tual rigidities, these gains are far from uniformly distributed within young cohorts:
they are systematically larger among permanent workers, workers in firms above the
employment-protection threshold, tertiary-educated workers, and workers in technolog-
ically advanced sectors. The resulting disparities in retention probabilities point to an
important distributional dimension of technological change, with potential implications
for within-cohort inequality.

detail.abstract: Radar-based human activity recognition does not require identifiable images, making it attractive for low-light, occluded, and privacy-sensitive scenarios such as home monitoring. . However, existing fully supervised methods for continuous activity recognition depend  on frame-level ground-truth labels, whose annotation is costly and labor-intensive. To address this issue, this paper presents WS-RPATCN, a two-stage framework for weakly supervised temporal action segmentation that uses only action transcripts as annotations and requires no frame-level labels. In the first stage, statistical consistency within radar segments of the same action class is used to construct a joint physical–semantic energy function for global alignment. Under action-transcript constraints, dynamic programming searches for the optimal combination of boundary assignment, and backtracking yields frame-wise pseudo-labels. In the second stage, a dual-dilated temporal convolutional network with multi-stage refinement is trained on these pseudo-labels to produce frame-wise predictions.  On three splits of an in-house dataset, WS-RPATCN achieves mean Edit, F1@50, and accuracy of 94.89%, 95.14%, and 0.9256, respectively, with an accuracy of 0.9400 ± 0.0027 across independent runs.. Experiments on unseen action orders and the RCCSL-108, MSD and Glasgow datasets further demonstrate that the proposed method provides effective temporal supervision from  action transcripts alone, achieves segmentation performance close to that of fully supervised methods and substantially reduces annotation costs for radar sensing systems

detail.abstract: The matatu is Kenya's loudest argument that the market belongs to whoever can afford the gate. Eighteen million Kenyans earn their bread in the informal economy, and thousands of them drive, tout, park and ride inside a sector that competition law has declined to see. Saccos charge entry fees that dwarf a vehicle's daily takings. Route cartels sell stages as though they were title deeds. Regulators freeze new licences and call the freeze safety. Commuters and crews pay for every one of these. This article indicts that silence. It shows how cooperative form, regulatory mandate and informality launder cartel rents into lawful order, and it offers a mandate-margin test that separates what the state commands from what incumbents add. It tests the thesis against Kinatwa's Sh450,000 entry fee, the thirty-vehicle rule, the motorcycle boom and the 2026 licensing freeze, and reads South Africa's taxi inquiry as warning and invitation. It ends by demanding functional undertakings, open-access route concessions, impact assessments and enforcement that spares the poor and pursues the gatekeepers.

detail.abstract: We utilize a simple structural model to characterize the drivers of the expected buyand-hold return distribution of the cross-section of leveraged exchange-traded funds (LETFs). We find the cost of leverage to be the most important driver: the average 2× and 3× LETFs pay 1.26% and 1.62% more than the effective Fed funds rate annually, with substantial cross-sectional dispersion. Index autocorrelation also plays an important role as it directly impacts costs associated with rebalancing to maintain target leverage amounts. Contrary to practitioner wisdom and previous academic findings, "volatility drag" only harms buy-and-hold returns if the additional volatility is autocorrelated. Using estimated costs for a fund tracking the S&P 500, we consider a household's portfolio choices over a lifecycle with access to a leveraged equity fund. A representative household will hold the LETF at all stages throughout the lifecycle with portfolio weights ranging from 35% to 100%. Some LETF ownership is optimal for long-term investors and is currently accessible in some tax-advantaged retirement accounts.

detail.abstract: The construction of the Global Value Chain (GVC) has greatly benefited the world economy. However, the recent surge in geopolitical conflicts has raised concerns about the potential fragmentation of GVCs, making it crucial for countries to identify effective means of mitigating the adverse political and economic consequences. In this article, we develop a theoretical framework to examine how geopolitical shock risk affects participation in GVCs and to explore which factors may serve as potential moderators, and then, regressions based on a panel dataset of 77 countries covering 1995–2020 are conducted to seek empirical support. The baseline regressions, along with a series of robustness checks and endogeneity settlements, demonstrate that geopolitical shock risk indeed hinders GVC participation, whereas domestic financing convenience exerts a highly significant mitigating effect. Moreover, heterogeneity analyses based on marginal effects suggest that countries participating in different segments of the GVC interact with geopolitical conflicts in heterogeneous ways; in contrast, inter-sectoral level analyses highlight the strong consistency of the negative effects of geopolitical shock risk and the robust effectiveness of domestic financing convenience in alleviating such impacts.

detail.abstract: Asset-pricing theory predicts low risk premia in good times. We test this prediction with a physical measure of real activity: the carbon dioxide U.S. industry emits as it burns fuel. When industry runs hot, expected returns are low. A one-standard-deviation increase in emissions predicts a 4.2 percentage point lower market excess return over the next year. Emissions forecast returns out of sample up to five years ahead; at one year, their forecasts encompass those of 20 established predictors. Return decompositions trace the predictability to discount rates, not cash flows. Industry's carbon footprint thus tracks the price of risk.

detail.abstract: This paper develops a continuous-time real options model for professional football player contracts incorporating transfer windows, release clauses, and contract expiration. Unlike constant-intensity models, transfer offers arrive at a state-dependent logistic rate that responds to player performance and release fees. The resulting two-factor HJB framework captures a performance-retention trade-off: at fixed club revenue productivity, stronger performance increases both attributable revenue and exposure to transfer offers. Relative to a matched constant-intensity benchmark, the model reveals systematic valuation differences across performance levels. For high-contribution players, the constant benchmark overstates mandatory-transfer risk at lower performance levels and understates it for high-performing players. Under mandatory release clauses, higher performance can reduce contract value even at identical revenue contributions, producing a talent-induced valuation inversion. The associated release-clause valuation deficit widens from 17.97% to 40.13%. Transfer-acceptance thresholds also rise near window deadlines and contract expiration.

title: Purchasing Power Parity, Dutch Disease, and the Stand-Alone Value of a Petro-Currency: Estimating the Equilibrium Exchange Rate of the Iraqi Dinar
affiliations: Nidaba Capital Hub

detail.title: Purchasing Power Parity, Dutch Disease, and the Stand-Alone Value of a Petro-Currency: Estimating the Equilibrium Exchange Rate of the Iraqi Dinar

declarations.declarationOfInterest: there are no personal or financial relationship with other people or organizations that may have or could be perceived to have influenced their study
declarations.funderStatement: No one has funded this research

detail.abstract: Relative purchasing power parity (PPP) is only admissible as an equilibrium benchmark when anchored on a base year in which the exchange rate was set by the market rather than by the policy authority. For Iraq this rules out every year from 2004 onward, when the Central Bank of Iraq currency-auction window made the rate the administered outcome of an oil-dollar (and, until 2011, U.S. military-dollar) supply; the only admissible anchors are 2002 and 2003, before the window opened. Anchoring there and correcting for the two oppositely signed effects of foreign military expenditure, a demand channel that raised local prices and a dollar-supply channel that suppressed them; through a depreciation parameter δ swept across its plausible range, we estimate the dinar's stand-alone equilibrium (its value when the oil-dollar inflow is interrupted) at roughly 3,300-3,900 IQD/USD in 2023. We validate this estimate by three independent methods that use no PPP information: the currency's monetary backing M/R at survivable reserves (3,000-4,500); the balance-sheet reserve-depletion identity, under which a cumulative reserve loss d forces a devaluation of d/(1-d) (3,000-3,750 at a 40-50 percent loss); and the International Comparison Program price level. The four methods converge on 3,300-3,900 and jointly identify the strong-correction region of the δ sweep (in-country expenditure share ψ ≈ 0.8-1.0) as the economically correct one. By contrast, the uncorrected 2002-anchored benchmark of about 9,000 is an artifact of a sanctions-depressed anchor and of a Balassa-Samuelson/Dutch-disease real appreciation that is entirely non-tradable and oil-financed. The market value conditional on the flow is simply the observed rate (official 1,320, street 1,555 in mid-2026), and the parallel premium; within a few percent for 2008-2019, easing in 2024-2025, and jumping to 18 percent under the 2026 Strait of Hormuz closure; confirms that the dinar's value tracks the flow, not its history of relative inflation. The dinar is not mispriced; it is contingent, and its stand-alone value near 3,300-3,900 is what binds when contingency is tested.

detail.abstract: This paper studies a collective decision problem in which a group of judges must select the deserving winner from a set of candidates. Judges agree on who deserves to win, but each judge may favor several candidates and wish to harm several others. The planner observes these conflicts of interest but neither the judges' exact preferences nor the identity of the deserving winner. Minimal neutrality, the requirement that every pair of candidates has a judge impartial between them, is necessary and sufficient for implementation via backward induction. We propose sequential mechanisms that rely only on candidate announcements: an announcement in favor of a candidate the judge favors is disregarded, and any other announcement progressively reduces the set of eligible candidates. The construction gives local conditions linking the candidates discarded and the judges consulted to the known pattern of conflicts of interest. Any mechanism assembled from rounds satisfying these conditions selects the deserving winner in every backward induction equilibrium. One such round, which discards a single candidate by default, is always available under minimal neutrality. No further structural relation among the judges' friend and enemy sets is required. The framework accommodates distinct judges and candidates, and richer jury configurations allow rounds that discard several candidates at once or involve only one or two judges.

title: The Flight-to-Quality in Office Real Estate: Evidence from London

detail.title: The Flight-to-Quality in Office Real Estate: Evidence from London

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The authors declare that they have no conflicting interest

detail.abstract: We examine how the performance of higher-quality offices in London evolved following the Covid-19 pandemic, relative to lower-quality stock. Using submarket-year data from CoStar spanning 2003-2025, together with the CoStar Building Rating System, we implement a differencein-differences framework comparing 4-and 5-star office properties to 3-star properties before and after 2020. We find that higher-quality offices experienced significantly higher asking rents but also higher vacancy rates, alongside a marked contraction in transaction activity. Disaggregating our treatment group by individual star rating shows that rents rose and vacancy fell for 5-star properties specifically, while the increase in vacancy was concentrated among 4-star properties. We document a parallel geographic divergence, with the transaction-market contraction concentrated in Central London & Docklands and the rise in vacancy more pronounced in Outer London. Our results indicate that the pandemic did not benefit high-quality office stock uniformly, but instead accelerated a more selective reallocation of demand toward the very best assets in the most central locations.

title: Dynamic Identification of Sovereign Facilitators in International Corporate Tax Avoidance

detail.abstract: International corporate tax avoidance is facilitated by sovereign jurisdictions that function as tax havens, financial secrecy havens, or offshore financial centres. The active policies of these jurisdictions potentially erode the tax basis of other countries, create an uneven playing field for domestic and multinational firms, and undermine international fiscal cooperation. However, the definition and identification of such sovereign facilitators of tax avoidance is --in both policy documents and academic literature-- surrounded by a lack of agreement. Traditional lists of tax havens are seldom updated, have no time variance, and often ignore tax havens among rich countries. This paper proposes the Joint Dynamic Identification Framework (JDIF), a standardised method that simultaneously identifies tax havens, financial secrecy havens, and offshore financial centres. Using only five statistical indicators makes it easy to apply this identification tool. We present a full-fledged proof-of-concept, covering the period 2001-2022 and more than 200 jurisdictions. The JDIF method shows that the pattern of border-crossing corporate tax avoidance is highly dynamic. Individual jurisdictions sometimes change their specialisation in tax avoidance networks. The JDIF method reveals shifting patterns between groups of tax-avoidance-facilitating jurisdictions and generates data that can be used in network analysis. Several robustness tests show the validity of our findings and demonstrate its policy relevance.

declarations.declarationOfInterest: No Conflict of interest between Author

detail.abstract: Purpose. This case study examines how sustainable tourism theory can be operationalised through the participation of women in the development of green tourism villages (desa wisata hijau) on Lombok Island, West Nusa Tenggara. Design/methodology. The study adopts a qualitative, interpretive case design based entirely on secondary data: fifteen 2025-2026 publications by the lead author and colleagues on Lombok tourism villages, one recent publication by each co-author, and official reports from UNWTO, the Indonesian tourism-village network (Jadesta), Statistics Indonesia (BPS) and the Ministry of Cooperatives and SMEs. Documents were analysed through structured document analysis and thematic synthesis, with an explicit gender lens. Findings. The village economies documented in the corpus rest on activities in which women are commonly engaged: handicrafts and weaving, home-based culinary production, agro-processing and hospitality services. However, women are almost never named as actors in the reviewed studies, which instead attribute village capacity to generic categories such as 'the community', Pokdarwis or MSMEs. National data show that 77.8% of registered tourism villages remain at the pilot (rintisan) stage, while women make up 54% of the global tourism workforce and 64.5% of Indonesian MSME operators. The study proposes a Women-Centred Green Tourism Village (WGTV) framework linking women's roles to the environmental, economic and socio-cultural pillars of sustainability through four enablers. Originality. The paper re-reads a local body of applied tourism research through a gender lens and turns the observed 'gender invisibility' into testable propositions. Limitations. Conclusions are inferential and require validation with primary, sex-disaggregated field data.

detail.abstract: On 15 October 2026, MSCI launched a consultation on reclassifying Indonesia from Emerging Market to Standalone Market status-a two-tier downgrade that bypasses Frontier status-with a final decision due no later than 30 June 2027. This study extends the author's earlier analysis with three objectives: (1) to trace the governance-failure mechanisms that moved Indonesia's stock market from an index freeze (January 2026) to a proposed exclusion (October 2026); (2) to audit and update the author's technical simulation of monetary and fiscal impacts and to simulate a June 2027 Standalone scenario; and (3) to compare the evolution of stock exchange governance in the United States, the European Union/United Kingdom, Japan, Australia, and South Korea across four periods (1995-2026). The study uses an embedded single-case design that combines analysis of primary documents (MSCI, OJK, Bank Indonesia, and the Ministry of Finance), comparative institutional analysis, and quantitative simulation based on a workbook replica ted cell by cell (208 formulas). Four findings emerge. First, a normalized composite manipulation index ranks DSSA, BREN, and CUAN as the three highest-risk issuers-precisely the three issuers linked to the IDR 2.1 trillion OJK sanctions of 16 October 2026. Second, outcomes as of October 2026 exceeded the May 2026 pessimistic scenario for the JCI (5,185 vs. 5,800), the BI-Rate (5.75% vs. 5.25%), and foreign net selling (IDR 88.19 trillion vs. IDR 80 trillion), whereas foreign exchange reserves and the fiscal deficit proved more resilient. Third, Standalone reclassification could trigger passive outflows of USD 3-6 billion and active outflows of up to USD 15 billion, equivalent to 13.5% of foreign exchange reserves. Fourth, the transfer of a 30.25% stake in Bayan Resources at a 79.9% discount to the market price illustrates the price-discovery gap at the core of MSCI's concerns. The study recommends a credibility-restoration roadmap built on law enforcement and verifiable indicators ahead of the 30 April 2027 consultation deadline.

detail.abstract: The government is obliged to provide quality, fast, easy, affordable and measurable services. However, in practice, there is often a gap between public expectations and the reality of the service time of population administration documents. This article aims to uncover the root of the problem of delays in population administration services by using the Fishbone Diagram (cause-and-effect diagram) as the core method and the 5 Whys technique as a complement. Based on the synthesis of empirical data from the Population and Civil Registration Office (Disdukpencapil) of Pelalawan Regency as the main foundation, which is strengthened by a comparison of operational constraints in Malang City and Gresik Regency, the results of the analysis conclude that the delay in document completion is not only caused by employee performance alone. The root of the problem comes from the accumulation of systemic problems in the aspects of Human, Method, Machine, Materials, and Environment. Targeted problem solving requires agencies to intervene directly at the root cause, not just to address the symptoms on the surface.

detail.abstract: How much of Iraq’s inflation do the exchange-rate peg and the currency window drive, once money growth, fiscal dominance, and world prices are controlled for? The Central Bank of Iraq sells dollars at an official rate, the peg, held below the market rate; the gap is the discount. On a new monthly dataset for 2007 to 2024, a vector error-correction model finds that the peg drives prices and the discount does not. A 1 percent rise in the official rate raises prices by 0.30 percent within a year and 0.65 percent in the long run; the official rate leads prices in Toda-Yamamoto tests and explains nearly half of their forecast variance at two years, and it carries the market rate with it, by 0.80 percent within a year. Holding the market rate fixed, the official rate has no short-run effect, and when the Bank widened the discount in 2023, prices did not fall. Base money and world prices add little, and base money grows through the Bank’s purchases of oil dollars, not its lending to the Treasury. The discount transferred about $19.0 billion to window buyers over 2007 to 2021, with no detectable share reaching consumers.

title: Climate Risk Spillovers and Sovereign Financing
affiliations: Humboldt University Berlin and Humboldt University of Berlin

detail.title: Climate Risk Spillovers and Sovereign Financing
detail.abstract: Climate change strains public finances through direct economic effects, yet interconnected economies also face indirect climate exposure via trade networks. These spillovers can amplify costs but are widely ignored. We systematically examine foreign climate risk transmission into sovereign financing conditions by mapping and quantifying local and spillover impacts through global value chain linkages. We use a simple static model of production networks to conceptualize climate effects on sovereigns via international spillovers. Deploying regression models for 75 countries (2000-2022), we exploit exogenous variation in temperature to estimate domestic and spillover impacts on financing conditions, measured by sovereign credit ratings. Results are threefold. First, local temperatures exhibit negative and heterogeneous impacts on ratings, with a 1°C anomaly implying an average 0.2 notch downgrade. Second, ignoring foreign climate spillovers underestimates total climate risk by 30%, most severely for cold and small open economies. Third, climate-driven rating changes imply a 36 basis point sovereign borrowing cost increase, of which 11 basis points are attributable to spillovers. Findings hold implications for investors and policymakers regarding asset valuation, climate adaptation and fiscal sustainability.

title: Response Procedures and Treatment-Contrast Portability in LLM Choice Data
affiliations: Hubei University of Economics, Hubei University of Economics, Hubei University of Economics and Hubei University of Economics

detail.title: Response Procedures and Treatment-Contrast Portability in LLM Choice Data

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The authors declare no potential conflicts of interest with respect to the research, authorship, and/or publication of this paper.
declarations.ethicsApproval: Ethical approval was not required because the study involved no human participants, human participant data, animals, or animal data. The empirical observations analyzed in the paper are outputs generated by the two LLM deployment/run environments described in the manuscript.
declarations.funderStatement: This research was supported by the 2025 National College Student Innovation Training Program (Project No. 202511600019); Hubei University of Economics through the 2017 New Faculty Research Start-up Fund (Project No. XJ17BS36) and the project “Research on Employee Incentive Mechanisms in Service Enterprises Based on Experimental Methods” (Project No. PYZX201901); the Department of Education of Hubei Province (Grant No. 20Y136); and Hubei University of Economics (Grant No. D20200006).

detail.abstract:
LLM experiments can generate large choice samples, and repeated calls can make fixed-procedure choice probabilities and treatment contrasts increasingly precise under a stable sampling process. That precision, however, does not ensure that the same treatment contrast is recovered under a different response procedure. An additive response-procedure control supports a treatment contrast common across procedures only when the procedure leaves that contrast unchanged. We formalize this requirement by distinguishing choice-level invariance from treatment-contrast portability. On the probability scale, portability permits the response procedure to enter as a common additive shift. When portability fails, an interacted specification separates the procedure-specific contrasts, while an additive specification reports a procedure-mixture contrast.

We test these restrictions in a fair-coin betting task using two recorded model-runtime cases, DeepSeek and Gemma. Six reported histories define the treatment profile, and normal/swapped response formats hold the underlying bets and stated payoffs fixed while jointly changing action order and action-code mapping. The data contain 5,400 generations, including 1,080 in the primary baseline comparison. Under the baseline instruction, both cases reject choice-level invariance and treatment-contrast portability. For Gemma, the Tails-choice contrast between histories reporting two and eight consecutive Heads is -0.967 under the normal format and +0.933 under the swapped format. An additive linear probability model that controls for response format reports -0.017, exactly the equal-weight mixture of those opposing procedure-specific contrasts. DeepSeek shows a less extreme but still nonconstant response-format shift across histories.

The procedure-specific treatment contrasts remain well-defined estimands, but the data do not support treating them as a single contrast common to the two response formats. When the procedures are pooled, the additive regression coefficient instead summarizes the response-format mixture represented in the design.

title: Global Hydropower Exposure to Rainfall Variability: Historical Estimates and the 2026/27 El Niño
affiliations: World Bank

detail.title: Global Hydropower Exposure to Rainfall Variability: Historical Estimates and the 2026/27 El Niño
detail.abstract: Hydropower is the generation technology most exposed to interannual climate variability. This paper estimates empirically that exposure at the country level and applies it to the 2026/27 El Niño season, using seasonal forecasts for precipitations. Output is measured as the capacity factor — generation divided by the installed fleet — using a plant-level capacity panel. On 4,853 country-year observations across 117 countries over 1981–2024, a 10 percentage-point shortfall in annual precipitation reduces the hydropower capacity factor by 4.57% in the year it occurs and by a further 3.22% in the year after, with the total impact of a shortfall sustained over two years reaching 7.65% (p < 0.001). Country-level elasticities can be estimated for 112 economies; 62 have a two-year response that is negative and significant at 5%. Translating the ECMWF seasonal forecast through these estimates gives a net change in hydroelectricity of -6.0 TWh in 2026 and +56.2 TWh in 2027 across the sample, with gross shortfalls of 54.6 and 30.9 TWh. Valued at the short-run marginal cost of the thermal generation that would replace them, those shortfalls cost US$3.8 billion and US$2.2 billion. A comparison with published country studies shows the limit of the global analysis based on precipitations only. The role of water storage, transboundary waters, and snow and glacier melt is not captured by the elasticities. And a hydrological drought that is severe for a power system can be invisible in an annual national total, either because it is concentrated in a few months or because it straddles the turn of the calendar year. As such, this analysis is meant to inform global assessment and prioritization, not country-specific forecasts and interventions.

detail.abstract: Local governments’ discretion over tax rates may be used strategically when politicians perceive that a tax burden falls differently across voter groups. We study this mechanism in the context of Germany’s property tax reform, which created exogenous variation in the tax across voter groups and municipalities by allowing states to adopt different property valuation models. Some federal states implicitly set a higher tax for rental properties than for comparable owner-occupied units. We show that, over an average post-announcement period of 3.6 years, municipal tax multipliers increased by 15 percentage points more when two conditions were met: municipalities were governed by homeowner-friendly parties and were located in states where tenants will face a higher tax base per square meter. By identifying political drivers behind sharp increases in German property tax multipliers in recent years, we provide causal evidence that higher-level governments’ tax-base choices change the electoral incentives governing local tax rates.

detail.abstract: Swiss law asks the Swiss National Bank (SNB) and the finance ministry to agree on profit distributions smooth over the medium term, yet the Confederation and cantons received CHF 6, 6, 0, 0, 3 and 4 billion for 2020 to 2025. I model the arrangement as an actuarial dividend strategy: a capped payout schedule applied each year to equity above provisions whose growth the SNB alone decides. Under the 2026 agreement, a year without payout before 2031 is about as likely as not, and uninterrupted payouts would need a reserve the size of the SNB's equity. Because the payout is capped, recipients could smooth it with a fund a tenth that size. Tying the provisions to a published loss quantile, and letting payouts continue against a moderately negative reserve, would improve on the agreement, judged by the payout-risk trade-off accepted in 2026, but would make payouts rise when the SNB sells foreign currency. Among 28 central banks, only the SNB combines a negotiated payout with a deduction set by the bank alone. Its revocable promise of a lower allocation can be credible because formal terms would cost it risk or control. De jure independence indices miss who controls such deductions.

detail.abstract: Using a unique dataset of 50 long-short smart beta factors with returns net of transaction costs, we construct a strategy that dynamically invests in factors based on past returns and covariances. The results demonstrate that this approach significantly outperforms a static 1/N benchmark in terms of risk-adjusted returns, even in the post-2000 period of declining factor premiums. The strategy's low turnover and cost-effective implementation address key practical concerns, providing a robust framework for successful factor timing after transaction costs. The results are robust to multiple specification choices, such as covariance shrinkage, training window length, and transaction cost levels.

detail.abstract: Many emerging economies tend to rely considerably on carbon-intensive sectors, exposing themselves to potential transition risk. This paper quantifies the impact of this risk and the role of various policies and policy designs in mitigating it. It does so with a two-country two-sector environmental dynamic stochastic general equilibrium model, where each “country” represents a bloc of advanced or emerging economies, respectively. The model includes real-world features such as financial frictions and financial and trade linkages across blocs. With it, we simulate climate policy in advanced economies, in the form of carbon taxes and tariffs, and international coordination around a minimum global carbon price. This paper identifies and quantifies important vulnerabilities among emerging economies to the implementation of climate policy in advanced economies.

detail.abstract: Whether artificial agents reach the Nash equilibrium of an economic game has become a load-bearing question for algorithmic markets and multi-agent AI. The existing literature establishes a robust yes for one behaviour, tacit collusion above the competitive benchmark, while painting a mixed picture for equilibrium play in general. We argue the more useful question is not whether but when language models reach Nash, and what instrument detects it. Using a heterogeneous, cross-machine testbed in which agents drawn from three distinct model families (Qwen 3.6, Gemma 4, Nemotron 3) interact across two physical servers, we run three classic games with analytically known equilibria: the p-beauty contest, the iterated Prisoner’s Dilemma, and a Braess-paradox routing game. We find a consistent pattern: agents reproduce the exact Nash equilibrium only when the decision reduces to selecting the lowest of a set of given payoffs (the Braess game with explicit option costs, where the paradoxical equilibrium is recovered to the unit), whereas every task demanding genuine strategic reasoning, level-k depth in the beauty contest, backward induction in the Prisoner’s Dilemma, or computing congestion from cost formulas, is met instead with a memorized or social heuristic that diverges from equilibrium, sometimes catastrophically. A simple contamination probe, inverting the beauty-contest parameter so the equilibrium moves from 0 to 100, exposes the apparent equilibrium “success” of the standard game as template recall: agents move in the wrong direction. Crucially, heterogeneous cross-family interaction surfaces strategic asymmetries that are invisible under self-play: Gemma 4 performs textbook end-game defection and exploits a trusting Qwen in the Prisoner’s Dilemma, while Qwen out-routes Gemma and Nemotron in the congestion game. We adopt normalized exploitability (ε-Nash) as the primary metric, and we identify four under-explored measurement instruments, surrogate (non-interacting) controls, output-space convergence as an equilibrium signature, true cross-family heterogeneity, and human+AI neural co-measurement, as the open ground this testbed is built to claim. All results are pilot-scale and intended as a proof of concept and a methodological scaffold rather than a definitive benchmark.

detail.abstract: We decompose corporate bond spreads into issuer, market, contract, vintage, maturity and liquidity components using daily marks for 1,066 floating-rate and 773 inflation-linked Brazilian debentures from April 2021 to August 2026, and backtest the resulting pricing equation in real time. Identification compares bonds of the same issuer in the same month, which is possible because 82% of floating-rate bond-months belong to issuers with more than one bond outstanding. The issuer accounts for 54% of the cross-sectional variance of floating-rate spreads and 56% of inflation-linked spreads, a share that holds out of sample; agency ratings explain 22% of it. Within issuers, maturity is priced in proportion to the issuer's spread, the apparent premium of secured bonds is selection, a tax exemption for infrastructure bonds is worth 1.10 percentage points, about 58% of its full value to a taxed individual, and callable bonds remain anchored to the spread at which they were issued. A multiplicative model with a dynamic issuer component, estimated by a Kalman filter with a rating-based prior and updated by sibling bonds, prices bonds over 53 out-of-sample months without using their own price history, with a median absolute error of 14 basis points, a calibration slope of 0.96 and correct interval coverage. A bond's own last price still forecasts better because bond-specific deviations are persistent; they mean-revert, but not enough to pay transaction costs. The issuer component predicts credit events with an AUC of 0.84.

detail.abstract: Complex public systems depend on transfers between specialized subsystems: physical resources move through infrastructure, claims move through communication channels, eligibility records move among agencies, and corrective obligations move between institutions. The performance of a subsystem at one location or procedural stage does not, by itself, establish the condition, meaning, or outcome of the larger sequence. This paper synthesizes a systems-based conceptual framework developed through longitudinal independent research beginning with drinking-water infrastructure and expanding to information governance, federal data interoperability, consumercomplaint classification, and oversight follow-up. Its organizing proposition is that transfer pathways may themselves change or obscure the state of what passes through them; accountability therefore requires attention to interfaces as well as individual organizations. Six dimensions—identity, provenance, constraint, transformation, causality, and recoverability—are Young · Governance Continuity Across Complex Systems · October 2026 | 2 developed as an assessment framework. Documentary illustrations are drawn from U.S. Environmental Protection Agency materials concerning premise plumbing, a 2026 Government Accountability Office report on federal eligibility-data interoperability, public Consumer Financial Protection Bureau descriptions of complaint outcomes, and GAO follow-up reporting. These sources document different kinds of boundary and closure problems; they do not establish a universal causal mechanism, prevalence, institutional intent, or wrongdoing. The study distinguishes valid procedural completion from verified substantive resolution and proposes a transparent coding protocol, rival explanations, negative cases, and prospective empirical tests. Its proposed contribution is a bounded, independently contestable framework for reconstructing what entered a system, what changed, which authority acted, what outcome was established, and what remains unknown.

detail.abstract:
Although rising global demand for critical minerals is widely expected enhance the position of resource rich states, most continue to export raw or minimally processed commodities, while high-value activities remain concentrated in other regions. This Thesis examines the conditions under which rising demand increases host-state bargaining power and enables economic upgrading within mineral value chains. 


The thesis argues demand is not sufficient for economic upgrading. Instead, demand is the starting point of a causal mechanism that operates through three necessary-but-not-sufficient conditions, each dependent on the preceding one: the transformation of demand into bargaining power, the translation of bargaining power into policy through policy autonomy, and the conversion of policy into outcomes via state capacity. A process-tracing comparison of Zambia (copper) and Indonesia (nickel) demonstrates that these cases diverge by progressing to different stages along this pathway. Zambia halts at the first condition, negotiating from a position of fiscal weakness and failing to convert demand into leverage. In contrast, Indonesia advances through all three stages, employing an export ban to mandate domestic processing, but achieves only limited upgrading, as value capture and ownership remain largely foreign controlled, 


This study foregrounds the state as an agent able to reposition itself within a value chain and refines each condition: bargaining power can be constructed through policy rather than inherited from resource endowment; policy autonomy requires the capacity to sustain a direction, not only to choose one; and state capacity is dimension-specific, so that localising an activity differs from capturing its value. Therefore, converting mineral demand into development requires a rare alignment of favourable market structure, durable policy autonomy, and multidimensional state capacity.

detail.abstract: Greece's sovereign debt was notably one of the most important fiscal and financial crises in the history of the euro zone. The crisis emerged from a compound of inordinate public borrowing, repeatedly fiscal deficits, sluggish economic growth, and systemic inefficiencies in public management and labour markets. By 2009, public debt had surpassed €300 billion, corresponding to about 130% of GDP, while modifications to official deficit data revealed years of fiscal misrepresentation and acutely impaired investor confidence. As sovereign bond yields surged and access to capital markets eroded, Greece needed consecutive international rescue schemes financed by the International Monetary Fund (IMF), European Union, European Financial Stability Facility (EFSF), and later, the European Stability Mechanism (ESM). The report uses analytical frameworks of sovereign-debt, which include debt-to-GDP ratios, fundamental balances, debt-drivers models, conditions of debt sustainability, net present value (NPV) analysis, as well as sovereign-bond spreads to assess the evolution of Greek debt level between 2009 and 2018. The analysis shows that Greece's debt distress stayed remarkably high through the period of crisis despite immense policy interventions. Public debt rose from nearly £300 billion in 2009 to more than €330 billion by 2018; in the same period, the debt-to-GDP leaped from 130% to nearly 181%, manifesting the joint impacts of falling output, recession, and sustained financing prerequisites. The defining occurrence of the crisis was notably the 2012 Private Sector Involvement (PSI) adjustment, which involved roughly €206 billion of sovereign bonds and sanctioned 53.5% nominal haircut on private investors, with evaluated NPV losses of approximately 75%. Despite the adjustment decreased the face value of debt, the benefits were partially neutralised by economic contraction and declining GDP. During the same period, Greece in piecemeal upgraded its fiscal level, shifting from deficits prior to 2013 to maintained primary surpluses beyond 2016. Debt negotiations centred progressively on maturity prolongations, concessional financing, including interest-rate cuts, resulting in a deep positive change in the ownership structure of Greece's debt, with authorised institutions becoming major creditors. The crisis had extensive effects for both Greece and the broader euro zone. Greece witnessed a cumulative GDP contraction surpassing 25%, unemployment went up to roughly 27% at its highest level, and the banking sector underwent acute losses that needed recapitalisation.

detail.abstract: Standard practice compares volatility constructions by how closely their implied-volatility curvature matches an observed or target smile. This comparison is methodologically compromised at the level of its object. This paper operationalizes it numerically across three market-standard constructions-Black-Scholes, SVI, and SABRunder two market regimes. We show, first, that there is a non-stably negligible component of any construction's curvature; second, that its relative weight is highly non-invariant across strike and across market condition; and third, that the pairwise ranking between constructions under this criterion is itself unstable-which construction appears to carry the smaller operator-induced share reverses at a non-trivial fraction of strikes simply by changing the volatility regime, with no construction dominating globally. No construction is exempt from the operator's contribution, and no stable preference ordering exists among them. We further show that this instability is not an artifact of the (K, σ) representation: it survives the change of coordinates at comparable frequency, while the specific points of instability shift. The result sharpens a conceptual objection into a demonstrable structural instability: comparing volatility constructions through curvature-matching does not identify a well-defined "better" model.

detail.abstract: We analyze the design of dynamic mechanisms without transfers. The designer uses future allocation decisions to elicit private information. Values evolve according to a two-state Markov chain. We solve for the optimal allocation rule, which permits a simple implementation: the agent is entitled to a number of units "no questions asked"; this number is reduced by one when he requests a unit and revised, although not necessarily upward, when he forgoes one. Unlike with transfers, inefficiencies are backloaded, and both immiseration and its polar opposite are possible long-run outcomes. In the continuous-time limit, we show that persistence hurts.
