detail.abstract: We develop a new methodology to identify bear and bull markets in the US stock market, which only relies on calibrating a bandwidth parameter around each trading day to define peaks and troughs. We find this bandwidth to be 8 months leading to bear (bull) market spells with a median duration of 74 (294) days and median cumulative returns of-16.2% (+37%). Within each stock market phase, we formulate a regime switching model differentiating between normal down, crash and recovery regimes within a bear market and normal up, risk-on and correction regimes within a bull market. The model has two special features: it focuses on mean regimes and uses cumulated returns rather than daily returns. A daily return model with common volatility and mean regimes performs very poorly. We further validate the model using statistical tests, textual analyses using Wall Street Journal articles and an anatomy of important stock market episodes.

detail.abstract: When does macroprudential policy become visible in bank funding structures? Using European bank-level data for 1996-2019, this paper examines funding-liquidity adjustment around two distinct stages of macroprudential intervention: policy announcement and effective implementation. We distinguish tightening from loosening and measure policy activity using both the occurrence and the number of policy actions. Funding liquidity is captured by three complementary bank-level measures reflecting the loan-deposit funding gap, deposit-based funding stability, and the loan-to-deposit ratio. The results show that the relationship between macroprudential intervention and bank funding liquidity changes over the policy cycle. Baseline estimates indicate stronger funding-liquidity positions close to tightening announcements, but these associations are sensitive to alternative inference procedures. More persistent patterns emerge after implementation. Tightening is initially associated with stronger funding liquidity but is followed by higher funding-liquidity exposure in subsequent years, while loosening is associated with a more immediate and persistent deterioration. These post-implementation patterns are particularly pronounced when policy is identified by its occurrence rather than the number of actions and remain visible after accounting for funding-liquidity persistence and alternative assumptions about residual dependence. Policy-response tests provide no systematic evidence that the fundingliquidity measures considered predict subsequent macroprudential announcements. Overall, the findings show that understanding the relationship between macroprudential policy and bank funding liquidity requires distinguishing when policy becomes effective, its direction, and how intervention is measured.

detail.abstract: This paper examines whether the principles that keep markets contestable and growth inclusive can restrain the legislator and the minister in Kenya and South Africa. Kenya's Supreme Court rejected the basic structure doctrine in 2022 while conceding that the Constitution has a structure. South Africa's Constitutional Court has never decided the question. Between those positions lies an unexplored problem: where does competition policy sit when entrenched text never names it? The paper advances a Derivative Structure Thesis. Competition commitments draw constitutional force from entrenched values, consumer rights and socioeconomic guarantees, and they are policed at three gates: amendment, legislation and executive action. Tested against the Competition (Amendment) Bill 2026, South Africa's public interest reforms, the Canal+ and MultiChoice conditions and the High Court's September 2026 nullification of the Safaricom sale, the thesis shows doctrine arriving late and discretion arriving early. Official unemployment of 33.6 per cent in South Africa and an informal share of 87 per cent of new Kenyan jobs expose the stakes. Seven concrete reforms follow from it.

detail.abstract:
This study critically assesses a 2010 proposition that Southwest and Near Southeast could become a second downtown for DC, comparable to existing downtown in land area and development square footage. It distinguishes development magnitude from measured functional concentration and structural form, comparing the reconstructed Southwest–Navy Yard Candidate Territory with three established-downtown DC benchmarks. The analysis uses employment, CAMA building-area records, hotels, and modeled Structural Intensity (SI), with a portable reproduction workflow and explicit sensitivity tests. The Southwest–Navy Yard Candidate Territory contains 928.1 land acres and 45,946 recorded workplace jobs in 2023: 76.5%–168.0% of benchmark land area but only 15.1%–21.7% of benchmark employment. Between 2010 and 2023, its all-jobs count declined 16.9%, while private jobs increased 25.0% and recorded federal jobs declined 43.9%. Federal reporting limitations prevent attributing that decline wholly to economic change. Mean SI reaches 44.6%–53.2% of benchmark levels.

At the primary threshold, 54.7% of its land cells qualify, versus 77.1%–83.2% across benchmarks; its largest connected share is 57.8%, versus 99.3%–99.6%. Lowering the threshold by 20% raises its largest share to 97.2%, demonstrating that the fragmentation contrast is threshold-dependent. Lower intensity and qualifying-cell coverage persist across the declared tests. Its CAMA-classified commercial-office subtotal is 35.18 million square feet of gross building area; the 2022 hotel snapshot contains 12 properties and 3,144 rooms. Evidence-family omission checks distinguish corroboration from shared-input dependence.

The measured functional and intensity differences do not support equivalence with established downtown DC; the cohesion conclusion is conditional on the primary specification. Civic, institutional, convention, meeting, and cultural functions are not comprehensively inventoried. These findings neither establish inevitable future equivalence nor conclusively reject the article’s longer-term development-capacity possibility.

detail.abstract:
The financing problem in AI infrastructure is not simply that chips become obsolete. It is that the site, equipment, customer promise and investor claim change on different timetables, often without an agreed source of money for the transition. This paper proposes the Cascade Estate: a permanent owner of powered facilities and selected computing equipment that sells a continuing, measurable service rather than the lasting value of a particular chip. Its central mechanism links two cycles. An operating cascade retains, reassigns or replaces equipment according to the complete cost of an accepted result. A financing cycle collects the service revenue, meets finite claims and funds required renewal before distributing the remaining cash. A proposed renewal covenant joins customer affordability, technical qualification and committed funding at the point of each new obligation, with independent verification and controls on order release. Power procurement, capacity rights and counterparty exposures are assessed within that same decision. Public transactions, supplier observations and established operating methods anchor the proposal; missing deal terms and future performance remain named, material assumptions. Thought experiments explain why idle capacity is not necessarily saleable, an upgrade is not automatically growth, and securitisation allocates rather than removes risk. The contribution is an integrated, testable architecture for making technological change financeable while preserving growth choices. It does not require speculative technology or claim a universally profitable estate.

detail.abstract: What is a tariff threat worth if it can be withdrawn within days? In his first term, President Trump imposed tariffs under trade laws that take months to apply and months to undo. In his second term, by contrast, he used emergency powers (IEEPA) that let him impose or cancel a tariff by executive order. Using 48 tariff actions and six major stock indices, we ask whether this faster instrument made tariff threats cheaper. We find that it did, but only once markets had seen IEEPA in use. A first-term tariff threat lowered the six indices by 0.66% over two days, while a second-term threat lowered them by only 0.02%. Early IEEPA threats, made before May 2025, cost as much as first-term threats, whereas later ones cost about a quarter as much. Tariff threats unsettled markets just as much in both terms, so a reversible threat costs less but remains a source of uncertainty. Finally, under IEEPA a reversal within five trading days lifted prices by 0.72% more than a slower reversal, which puts a price on what traders called the 'TACO' trade.

The implied allocation is far from the first-best. Welfare gains can be obtained in a setting in which private offsets are measured, verified, and tokenized into ‘green coins’ exchanged via a transparent ledger. Because of financing and fiscal frictions, this equilibrium is still inefficient. detail.abstract: Kenya's Judiciary has spent the current constitutional decade earning, and periodically deserving, its reputation as the branch most willing to tell the executive and the legislature the truth about their own conduct. This article asks what that reputation obscures. It traces two related but distinct patterns in the courts' own behaviour. The first is a recurring willingness to declare a law or an action unconstitutional while suspending, delaying, or otherwise softening the remedy that declaration would ordinarily compel, a pattern this article calls remedial evasion, adapting Karl Klare's diagnosis of a legal culture that prizes procedural correctness over transformative effect. The second, newer and more troubling, is a development in which individual judges facing removal petitions before the Judicial Service Commission have used the High Court's own conservatory-order jurisdiction to freeze the one constitutional mechanism built to hold them accountable. Read together, these patterns suggest that judicial independence and judicial self-interest are not always distinguishable in practice, and that a bench capable of checking the other two branches has not yet shown the same discipline in checking itself. The article closes by testing that claim against its strongest objection: that removal petitions can themselves be weaponised, and that a conservatory order is an ordinary tool of due process, not evidence of a guild protecting its own.

detail.abstract: Fed Chairs are partisan appointments, but do they behave as partisan policymakers? Presidents appoint the Chair of the Federal Reserve and later decide whether to reappoint. This paper examines whether Chairs repay the party that appointed them or ease policy to win reappointment. We model a Chair who may value loyalty and reappointment and show how to separate these motives from the information in presidential pressure. Using monthly data from 1960 to 2026, we find no evidence that Chairs set easier policy for the appointing party or in the year before a reappointment decision. Presidential pressure predicts modestly lower rates, but its effect does not depend on the Chair's career stake. Central bank heads in five other democracies show the same pattern. Chairs are partisan appointments but behave as nonpartisan policymakers.

detail.abstract: We examine whether lower CO₂ intensity and salient moral-account states shape allocations to an emissions-generating fund. In a randomized incentivized online experiment with 1,300 participants in Germany, we orthogonally vary fund type and the salience of prior environmentally responsible or insufficient behavior. At the gradual investment margin, assignment to the lower-CO₂, sustainability-positioned fund increases allocations. A descriptive calibration shows that the rebound-like response offsets 1.7% of the potential CO₂ reduction from the experimental intensity difference. Moral debt reduces gradual investment, consistent with moral cleansing, whereas moral credit exhibits a weakly supported increase in gradual investment but a lower full-allocation probability. The findings indicate cross-domain spillovers from prior environmental conduct to investment behavior and asymmetric effects across behavioral margins. Exploratory comparisons suggest that treatment patterns are not fully context-invariant.

detail.abstract: This paper studies how career dynamics shape teacher spatial sorting using data on Peru's centralized teacher allocation. I develop a dynamic two-sided matching model and identify teacher and school preferences from observed assignments and schools' discretionary evaluations. I use the estimated model to correct teacher value-added estimates for two-sided endogenous selection. The analysis reveals the existence of a spatial job ladder that dynamically sorts more effective teachers into urban schools, contributing to spatial inequality in student achievement. Targeted mobility restrictions can reduce the urban-rural effectiveness gap by 76 percent, but avoiding adverse selection requires compensating teachers for the implied welfare loss, highlighting an inherent recruitment–retention trade-off.

detail.abstract: A farmer considering a new perennial crop, or someone considering a new vaccine, may prefer to wait and learn from others' experience. I show that publicly committing to a temporary pause in access can accelerate adoption: some agents adopt earlier, and their experience informs those who wait. I characterize the access calendar that reaches an adoption target as soon as possible, for general smooth distributions of good-state payoffs. A pause must last long enough to keep early adopters from waiting until reopening. Each pause is compared with the gradual adoption it replaces. These time effects add across nonoverlapping pauses, so the optimal calendar selects the pauses that together save the most time. Continuous access until a final round is optimal when the payoff density is nonincreasing, whereas sufficiently strong local concentration can make pauses beneficial. For a fixed adoption population, faster completion need not raise welfare: a pause induces some agents to bear the risks of earlier experimentation and makes others wait longer. Heterogeneity in prior beliefs is equivalent to payoff heterogeneity, allowing the principal to use data on beliefs or gains to choose access dates.

detail.abstract: Governments spend millions on improving their country’s image but rarely know which perceptions relate to specific economic outcomes. This paper evaluates nine annual waves of a global perception survey covering 84 countries, 65 perception attributes, and over 15,000 respondents per year. The analysis distinguishes the economic outcomes of GDP per capita, foreign direct investment, exports, and tourist arrivals. Because perception attributes are multicollinear, they are clustered into seven coherent and interpretable dimensions: Governance, Development, Business, Livability, Culture, Power, and Low Cost. A two-level stacked ensemble, which combines cluster-level Bayesian Ridge regressions with a gradient-boosting meta-learner, relates these dimensions to the economic outcomes. The model explains 87% of the variation in exports and 84% in GDP and outperforms a Human Development Index (HDI) benchmark for foreign direct investment, tourism, and exports. The analyses provide specific direction to countries as to where they can most benefit economically from changes in how they are perceived.  For instance, the USA’s perception drop from 2024 to 2026 is associated with  6.5% lower GDP, 9.9% lower exports and 19% fewer tourist arrivals Rather than a country advertising its way to prosperity, though, the link to objective fundamentals points to what needs to change in reality, alongside perceptions.

detail.abstract: Disclosure theory predicts that public information brings analysts together. We study public information the firm does not control: being named a defendant in a lawsuit. Using 56,407 firm-years of analyst-covered U.S. firms from 2000 to 2024, we find that being sued raises analyst forecast dispersion within firm by about a third of the median, while being a plaintiff has no effect. The increase is not explained by thinner coverage, volatility, the news that triggers lawsuits, standing litigation risk, or the firm's prior 10-K disclosure, and instrumenting lawsuits with court geography yields estimates of the same sign. Disagreement persists while the case is open and ends at resolution, whether by settlement or dismissal. Uncertainty and idiosyncratic disagreement rise while consensus does not, and analysts shift away from buy recommendations. Public disclosure widens disagreement when it reveals an unresolved contingency rather than resolving one.

detail.abstract: Do major football tournaments move economic sentiment, and does it matter whether a country's national team takes part? We combine the European Commission's harmonized business and consumer surveys for the 27 EU member states from 1991 to 2025 with 17 World Cups and European Championships. The Economic Sentiment Indicator is about 2.3 points higher in tournament months than in other months of the same calendar year, but it is similarly elevated in the two months before; consumer confidence shows no robust pattern. Because the tournament calendar is common to all countries and almost all tournaments fall in even years, this association rests on 17 events and cannot be separated from a broader two-year rhythm in sentiment; relative to randomly drawn years, it is unusual before 2020 and marginal in the full sample (p = 0.08 to 0.14). Participation varies across countries and can be tested with full time fixed effects, under weaker assumptions. We find no statistically significant participation premium in the baseline specification and no participation-specific jump at kick-off in any specification; large premia are hard to reconcile with the data, smaller ones remain possible.

detail.abstract: We study the optimality of human groundwater extraction from many of the world’s 3,400 aquifers, where institutional or market failures may produce nonoptimal extraction decisions. We use remote sensing and economic data to estimate a dynamic model of water extraction for each aquifer, recover the discount factor that rationalizes observed groundwater extraction, and compare it against Ramsey and market benchmarks. Three- to four-fifths of aquifers are extracted more rapidly than is optimal, decreasing aquifer present value by several percent, and creating trillions of dollars in present value welfare losses. Policies that guarantee users constant water quantities indefinitely, through subsidies or prior appropriation, or policy rules that fully discount future extraction, generate larger welfare costs. A sustainable extraction path that maintains current fill forever generates meaningfully lower welfare than the optimal extraction path, because most aquifer stocks are already inefficiently low.

detail.abstract: Cooperation that relies on partner choice needs association: cooperators must meet cooperators more often than chance would give. How association scales with community size should depend on how information about partners travels. Private, fading memory predicts association proportional to 1/N when a responder can recognise only a bounded number of partners. A public score pooled across a community predicts no size dependence. A mixture predicts an intermediate slope that attens with size. This Stage 1 registered report xes a test before any outcome is computed. In public Stack Exchange records, association is the probability that the rst answerer is a recent contributor given a contributor asker, minus the corresponding probability given a pure asker, controlling for tags. We estimate its log log slope across eligible site-quarters and within sites as they grow from 1,000 to 100,000 active users, using a positive-mean nonlinear estimating equation with count-based weights and a wild cluster bootstrap-t. We repeat a prespecied secondary design for review and help interactions in GitHub repositories recorded in GH Archive. The estimators, equivalence margin, six-row decision rule, precision gate and sixteen secondary analyses are xed in advance. A slope within 0.15 of zero supports the pooling prediction; one within 0.15 of-1 supports the bounded-memory prediction; an intermediate slope is consistent with a mixture but does not by itself identify its crossover.

detail.abstract: This paper examines whether and how foreign acquisitions improve occupational safety. Using linked administrative data on French manufacturing plants over 2003-2017 and event studies on a matched sample, we find that foreign acquisitions reduce accident rates and workdays lost. Safety gains coincide with expanded managerial hierarchies, greater technical-manager presence, foreign manager hiring, and worker training. We find little evidence supporting automation, task reallocation, or outsourcing as alternative explanations. Moreover, domestic acquisitions do not generate comparable improvements. Our findings are consistent with foreign acquisitions improving workplace safety through the transfer of managerial and organisational practices, highlighting a benefit of multinational activity beyond conventional measures of firm performance.

detail.abstract: Using Danish administrative data from 1980–2023, we analyze lifetime income (both earnings and net-income) inequality and its evolution across cohorts. Earnings inequality rises with age from midlife onward and is highest among the low educated and lowest among those with medium education. Differences in employment attachment — such as non-employment and part-time work — account for 30–60 percent of lifetime earnings dispersion, and are particularly important among the low educated. Lifetime earnings inequality has risen across cohorts among the low educated, partly through growing dispersion in employment attachment. In moving from earnings to net-income, transfers account for roughly five times as much of the inequality reduction as taxes, but this equalizing effect has weakened over time. Our results highlight the role of employment dynamics and social insurance for lifetime inequality.

detail.abstract:
The integration of Artificial Intelligence (AI) and Clinical Decision Support Systems (CDSS) within modern healthcare systems has fundamentally revolutionized the diagnostics and clinical prescription landscape. While AI-driven algorithms drastically minimize structural human errors, optimize multi-drug therapeutic configurations, and calculate complex pharmacokinetic parameters, they simultaneously create unprecedented systemic challenges within the domain of pharmaceutical jurisprudence. This interdisciplinary medico-legal manuscript addresses a critical and legally unmapped vacuum within the South Asian legal framework, specifically focusing on Bangladesh, India, and Pakistan: the assignment of civil and criminal liability when an AI diagnostic algorithm suggests an erroneous prescription, fatal drug-drug interaction, or incorrect dosage configuration that passes through a medical practitioner and a dispensing clinical pharmacist, resulting in severe patient morbidity or mortality.
From a clinical pharmacy perspective, the manuscript explores the algorithmic mechanisms governing computerized clinical decision-making and details how training data biases or software glitches cause drug allocation anomalies. From a legal standpoint, the analysis rigorously evaluates classical doctrines of medical negligence, product liability, and vicarious liability. It explores whether an AI system can be classified as a product or a service, and dissects the complex triadic relationship of liability shared among the software development corporation, the diagnosing medical practitioner, and the final dispensing clinical pharmacist who acts as the ultimate human safety filter. The empirical findings reveal an alarming absence of statutory legal guidelines or specialized regulatory frameworks across South Asian healthcare systems, exposing practitioners to disproportionate liabilities. Ultimately, this paper outlines a comprehensive, structured legislative framework proposal designed to redefine accountability and balance technological innovation with public safety.

detail.abstract: Artificial intelligence changes cyber defense through two simultaneous channels: it can increase the productivity of detection and investigation, while also reducing the time, expertise, and marginal effort required to generate adversarial activity at scale. Existing research has separately examined AI-enabled cyber economics, alert fatigue, risk-based alert prioritization, human-AI triage, and queue-constrained security operations. This paper asks a narrower operationaleconomic question: when does a gain in defensive unit productivity fail to improve system-level security because investigation-worthy adversarial arrivals grow faster than the defender's capacity to resolve them? We develop a capacity-frontier model in which adversarial arrival intensity, alert-admission policy, and effective investigation throughput jointly determine utilization, delay, and unresolved malicious burden. We ground the problem in published production-SOC evidence, including a four-year USENIX Security study of 115.6 million alerts, and in current BIS and IMF analyses identifying speed and scale as central AI-era cyber risks. A reproducible computational experiment then maps the defensive throughput required to preserve explicit service objectives under adversarial scaling. The experiment is not presented as production evidence; all parameters not externally observed are labeled simulated. The central managerial result is that AI-security investment claims should be stress-tested against workload elasticity rather than evaluated only from per-alert productivity. A tool that reduces investigation time can improve a local productivity metric while leaving the organization with higher utilization, longer malicious-case delay, or greater unresolved burden if adversarial arrivals expand sufficiently. The paper therefore proposes a practical Defensive Capacity Frontier for deciding whether marginal investment should go to admission quality, investigation throughput, upstream prevention, or reserve capacity.

detail.abstract: Factual auditing can detect falsification while leaving accurate but selectively chosen metrics undetected. We solve Bayesian allocation with private quality and metric-selection costs, then optimize random auditing of positive evidence packets. The equilibrium distinguishes all-submit inflation, inflation/non-submission mixing and metric-only reporting. Submitted and passed masses differ, and failed checks can still lead to funding. We derive a finite global candidate set from regime boundaries and stationary equations. Convexity excludes an interior welfare maximum in the mixing regime, whereas an all-submit regime can have an optimal partial audit with residual inflation. The resulting information and resource frontier is compared with no evidence and locked metrics. Results are restricted to the stated evidence menu and uniform-cost technology; computations are synthetic.

detail.abstract: Personal demand for generative AI connects workplace adoption to household budgets. We study this connection in eleven weekly ConsumerInsight surveys from South Korea, comprising 8,800 records and a main occupational sample of 4,440. Joint work and personal use is associated with substantially more widespread willingness to allocate a monthly AI budget. After adjustment for demographics, occupation, firm size, workplace policy and use frequency, the mixed-use differences reproduce in nine later waves at 11.3 percentage points relative to no work use and 8.5 points relative to work without personal use. A seven-configuration decomposition shows a further 4.6-point difference when study joins work and personal uses. The monetary ranking also holds in the full occupational sample after covariate adjustment and every admissible completion of incomplete amounts: at KRW 10,000, the later-wave mixed-use differences are bounded below by 4.2 and 2.6 points. Affirmative subscription-expenditure records are concentrated among work users, who account for 92.2% of these records against 73.8% of the comparable core sample. A net-value framework explains how benefits across purposes enter personal budgets relative to free and organizational alternatives. The findings establish purpose breadth as a substantial dimension of AI financing demand and place household budget decisions alongside organizational adoption in explaining the formation of a paying market.

detail.abstract:
Contemporary Artificial Intelligence in Education (AIED) and Intelligent Tutoring Systems (ITS) face a dual infrastructural and pedagogical crisis. Infrastructurally, cloud-hosted Large Language Models (LLMs) and dense Deep Knowledge Tracing (DKT) networks impose severe memory-bandwidth bottlenecks (4–80 GB VRAM), high latencies (>300 ms), privacy risks, and stochastic hallucinations. Pedagogically, systemic educational transformation frameworks grounded in chaos and complexity theory (Reigeluth, 2008) posit that learner empowerment and cognitive disequilibrium are prerequisites for self-organization; however, unconstrained self-directed learning consistently triggers the Saturn School Paradox (Bennett & King, 1991; Reigeluth, 2008), where autonomous self-direction without mathematical boundary damping collapses time-on-task and mastery retention.

We introduce Procedural Fractal Pedagogy (PFP), realized via the open-source WerreduR cognitive reflex engine. PFP formalizes Vygotsky's Zone of Proximal Development (ZPD) and Reigeluth's disequilibrium corridor as an explicit Observer Horizon Corridor anchored at sub-boundary resonance shoulder loci X_upper/lower = (0.25, ±0.18) along the boundary of the Mandelbrot set (∂M, z_{n+1} = z_n^2 + c). Individualized adaptive curricula are synthesized on demand from a 24-byte student coordinate seed Θ = (c_x, c_y, zoom) with O(1) constant memory complexity (0 Bytes persistent VRAM). To eliminate Saturn School learner drift and interior rote stagnation, PFP deploys an Information-Theoretic Semantic Token Damping Filter (T_desc = 0.045), a Biomimetic Perturbed Jump Operator (Ω_tunneling), and a Multi-Scale Harmonic Tripod kernel. Refuting the classical Fallacy of Erasure in scalar grading, student assessment is formalized as a unitary, non-dissipative error-kernel invariant (K_error ≅ I_3 = {0, 3, 6} ⊂ Z/9Z) under TAMAMe Horizon Complementarity B(t) + S(t) = 1, machine-verified in Lean 4 with zero sorry axioms.

Across N = 1,000 self-directed trajectories (T = 120 instructional cycles), unconstrained Saturn School self-direction collapses to 11.68% ± 0.31% time-on-task, whereas WerreduR achieves 94.19% ± 0.14% time-on-task (+82.51 pp vs. Saturn, p = 4.86e-11; +5.23 pp over Cloud LLMs, d = 1.54), 89.24% ± 0.13% ZPD residence, a 339.4x suppression in cognitive burnout stress (1.29 vs. 437.84), and a median decision triage latency of 2.32 ± 0.01 ms (134.5x faster than Cloud LLMs) with zero persistent VRAM.

detail.abstract: Question 75 of Treasury's proposed rule implementing section 3 of the GENIUS Act asks first how section 3 will affect US financial institutions in crossborder payments in foreign-currency stablecoins (or simply "tokens") issued abroad, and next, what changes would support that use while preserving foreign interest in comparability under section 18. On the first question, a problem seems to arise from an inconsistency between technical and legal objectives. That is, a bank that moves a foreign token through its wallet to complete a customer's payment does not offer, sell or make that token available in the US. Therefore, the final rule would benefit from stating this expressly. Absent that clarification, the bank could handle only tokens whose issuers have met the lawful-order condition in section 3(b)(2). Notably, it is respectfully submitted that foreign issuers may be slow to meet this condition without a reciprocal arrangement, even as the same tokens continue to enter the US through exempt peer-to-peer transfers. On the second conundrum, a survey of six jurisdictions that have adopted or proposed stablecoin rules since the GENIUS Act became law finds little provision for comparability. This seems to be because a dollar-denominated token brings US authority into a host's market. For example, such a token can be frozen on a US order. Consequently, without global standards that separate what a token can technically do from who controls it and who answers for its failures, it may be expected that host countries will continue to respond defensively. With no arrangement yet made under section 18, it is therefore recommended that the G7/G20 mandate the Financial Stability Board (FSB) to engage the Committee on Payments and Market Infrastructure (CPMI) and the International Organization of Securities Commissions (IOSCO) to establish a baseline standard for payment stablecoins on which mutual recognition can be built, and that the US join in this mutual recognition where warranted.

detail.abstract: Organization theory routinely lets designed structures (roles, routines, capabilities, technologies, contracts) explain outcomes while treating the processes that keep those structures efficacious as outside the explanation. We argue that this practice, which we call the design illusion, is a specific and diagnosable explanatory error rather than a general failure to notice recursion. It occurs when the maintenance of an explanatory structure is itself shaped by the outcome being explained within the explanatory horizon. To correct it we develop a typed theory of organizational closure adapted from the closure-of-constraints tradition in biological autonomy theory. We distinguish restriction relations, through which relatively conserved constraints narrow the feasible trajectories of faster processes, from maintenance relations, through which processes sustain those constraints, and we type maintenance relations by the mechanism that makes them operate: intentional reinforcement, selection, byproduct reproduction, and power or legitimation. We ground constitutive claims in time-scale separation, which resolves the problem that interventions on mutually maintaining systems cannot hold other components fixed, and we define an architectural premium that measures how much a constraint matters through maintenance propagation beyond its direct effects. The theory yields seven propositions that make predictions differing from those of coupling, capability-trap, reproduction-mechanism, and routine-dynamics accounts, concerning the allocation of maintenance, the sequencing of transformation, critical thresholds of temporal exposure, and the endogeneity of legitimacy thresholds. A documented case and a stylized simulation show that temporal exposure produces discontinuous, topology-dependent collapse. An extended illustration, the automation of junior work in a law firm, shows that closure theory and its rivals in agency theory and transaction cost economics pose different decision problems: the rivals optimize over end states, whereas closure theory constrains the transition path between them. Design survives, reinterpreted as one mechanism of maintenance operating from within the architecture it alters.

detail.abstract: Implementation order trades off better diagnosis against the option to avoid sunk remediation costs. We solve a binary learning and entry-certificate model with endogenous production experimentation, direct remediation and no remediation. Under the stated information ordering and equal assigned pilot costs, tools-first dominates all alternatives exactly on an open physical-cost interval. Closed-form cutoffs identify its competitors and the pilot-cost ceiling for nonemptiness. Synthetic primitives yield the full certificate-fee partition, all ties and an explicit reset threshold at which the interval disappears. Known repair, an independent reset and revealing public validation retain their Bayesian nulls. The contribution is a model-specific cost and fee characterization, supported by complete proofs and executable checks; no firm data are analyzed.

detail.abstract: Correlated evidence can make efficient research privately unattractive both initially and at continuation. In a two-case, two-slot model with expiration and optional terminal action, we derive the exact implementation and funding frontier for two nonnegative public-history credits. One rewards the initial experiment; the other rewards a specified contingent final experiment. Complete backward induction gives necessary and sufficient inequalities, separate expected and pathwise gross-funding limits, and attainment boundaries on a certified interval of binary priors. Credits are transfers rather than resource losses. The independent benchmark retains the recoverability-versus-priority comparison and common-charge classification. Complete proofs and exact synthetic enumeration support this restricted implementation result; no unrestricted mechanism optimum or empirical effect is claimed.

detail.abstract: The rapid expansion of the digital economy has fundamentally transformed traditional retail structures into interconnected, data-driven e-commerce ecosystems. In emerging Southeast Asian markets, enterprises increasingly operate across fragmented digital storefronts, including marketplace platforms (e.g., Shopee, Lazada, Tiki) and social commerce channels (e.g., TikTok Shop). However, managing multi-channel e-commerce operations presents critical challenges in inventory synchronization, dynamic pricing, warehouse fulfillment, and customer retention. This paper proposes an integrated conceptual framework that examines how Artificial Intelligence (AI) and big data analytics optimize e-commerce platform operations within the broader macroeconomic context of the digital economy. By synthesizing theoretical perspectives from Transaction Cost Economics (TCE) and the Resource-Based View (RBV), the study analyzes four core operational dimensions: (1) algorithmic pricing and promotional elasticity across platforms, (2) AI-assisted warehouse and last-mile logistics optimization, (3) automated customer journey personalization, and (4) digital payment risk management. The findings suggest that integrating predictive AI tools into e-commerce back-end operations reduces order fulfillment latency and mitigates multichannel inventory distortion (the bullwhip effect). This study provides actionable strategic insights for e-commerce operations managers, digital economists, and policymakers aiming to foster sustainable digital trade infrastructure.

detail.abstract: As large language models (LLMs) become gateways to digital services, they may reshape how consumers discover sellers and how sellers compete. We study the economic impact of this shift by examining ChatGPT's February 2026 integration with OpenTable, an online restaurant reservation platform. Using daily reservation availability data from January 3 to April 18, 2026, we compare restaurants on OpenTable and Resy, a comparable non-integrated platform, in a difference-indifferences design. We find no significant effect on average demand for OpenTable restaurants, but substantial redistribution across restaurants. Restaurants with more cumulative reviews, typically a positive signal in human-driven discovery, experience demand losses relative to counterparts unaffected by the integration. In contrast, restaurants with textually richer reviews accessible to AI experience larger demand gains. Average ratings do not significantly moderate these effects. We further estimate restaurant-level heterogeneous treatment effects using a doubly robust estimator and find larger effects for restaurants with more distinctive characteristics and dining goals. Evidence on mechanisms reveals changes in both consumer search and restaurant recommendations: consumers express more free-form, intent-rich search criteria when interacting with AI, while AI surfaces restaurants differently from the platform's conventional recommendation algorithms. Our findings suggest that AI-mediated search can change the basis of competition among sellers by reshaping which information guides discovery and how demand is allocated.

detail.abstract: Artificial Intelligence has revolutionised cybersecurity. It has transformed the domain of digital forensics. Its dual-use architecture engenders both challenges and unprecedented opportunities. This research critically examines the intersection of AI, privacy, security, cybercrime, and computer forensics. On one hand, AI fortifies cryptographic automation, and cyber threats detection. Concurrently, it facilitates hyper-sophisticated attack vectors, evasion, and forensic obfuscation, posing significant concerns. Existing literature extensively addresses AI-driven cybersecurity solutions. It discusses the admissibility of digital evidence, but it fails to systematically analyse AI’s adversarial implications for forensic integrity and legal frameworks. This study aims to bridge this research gap by assessing role of AI in threat mitigation and forensic automation while identifying vulnerabilities exploited through deepfakes, adversarial machine learning, and AI-assisted cybercrime. The study employs a doctrinal legal methodology. It conducts a comparative analysis of global regulatory instruments, and case laws. This study scrutinises AI’s impact on digital evidence authentication and procedural fairness. Preliminary results indicate AI-driven forensics yields promising results in anomaly detection, behavioural analysis, and automated evidence classification, yet adversarial AI undermines evidentiary reliability by enabling sophisticated data manipulation and attribution challenges. Jurisprudential analysis reveals inconsistencies in statutory and judicial approaches to AI-induced forensic complexities, necessitating harmonised regulatory frameworks. This study underscores the imperative for AI-specific evidentiary standards, adversarial-resilient forensic methodologies, and cross-border legislative convergence to enhance digital justice. The findings contribute to policy formulation by advocating for AI governance mechanisms balancing innovation with forensic robustness. Future research should explore quantum-proof encryption, AI liability frameworks, and real-time adaptive forensic techniques to counter emergent AI-facilitated cyber threats effectively.

detail.abstract: Firms can use generative AI to simulate customer responses before exposing real customers to alternatives, reducing regret from human experimentation at the cost of computation. However, synthetic responses may be biased, and correcting this bias requires information from human interactions. We study this tradeoff in a sequential experimentation model over a horizon of  $T$ periods. In each period, a firm offers one of $N$ alternatives (arms) to an arriving customer and observes a binary outcome. Before each human interaction, the firm may also purchase any number of synthetic evaluations by presenting alternatives to an AI simulator and observing its binary responses. We model the unknown difference between human and synthetic log odds of success as a linear function of the alternatives' features and an unknown bias vector. The features describe dimensions along which synthetic responses may be biased, while human response probabilities remain unrestricted across alternatives. We develop a calibration algorithm that learns the bias from matched human-synthetic experiments and uses the estimated bias to correct synthetic evaluations.  When the feature space has effective dimension $r$, for sufficiently large horizons, our policy achieves total regret $ O(\sqrt{rT}+(\gamma N)^{1/3}T^{2/3})$, where $\gamma$ is the unit cost of synthetic feedback. This can improve on the $\Theta(\sqrt{NT})$ regret of learning from humans alone when synthetic feedback is sufficiently inexpensive. We establish matching lower bounds up to logarithmic factors. Thus, synthetic data are most valuable when their bias can be explained by relatively few features. We further consider a setting with a large set of candidate bias features in which at most $k$ components of the bias vector are nonzero.  We show that, under suitable conditions, a Lasso-regularized version of our algorithm achieves regret $ O(\sqrt{kT}+(\gamma N)^{1/3}T^{2/3})$, without knowing in advance which features explain the bias.

detail.abstract:
Corporate directors are talented and experienced individuals who have been recruited to provide governance oversight to both for-profit and non-profit corporations. In addition to their track record of proven expertise, the common denominator for almost all veteran corporate directors is that they are constantly challenged to efficiently allocate their scarce resource of time. Perhaps the most difficult topic for almost all corporate boards is the governance of cybersecurity. Corporate boards tend to seek out: former CEOs; those experienced in management; marketing; finance; audit and domain expertise. Few corporate directors are experts in computer science or have a background in cybersecurity. Law and regulation is constantly challenged to keep pace with rapidly changing technological developments, with cybersecurity remaining a particularly vexing problem. While highly technical in nature, this exposure draft is valuable not only to those on the front line of day-to-day cyber defense ̶ but also provides useful information to corporate directors who must govern this complicated area of risk.

The National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST) represents a valuable potential resource of information for corporate directors.  This Article provides an introduction and overview of the unique services provided by various divisions of the NIST.  This Article provides insight into many technical aspects of the rapidly changing world of cyber vulnerabilities and assists directors in obtaining background knowledge necessary to engage in meaningful dialogue with their corporate talent responsible for cyber protection.
